# 🗽 Locality Research Guide: New York City, 1700s Colonial Period

**Jurisdiction surveyed:** New York City (standardPlace: *New York, New York, United States*)
**Target period:** 1700–1800 (British colonial era)
**Survey date:** 15 September 2026

---

## Jurisdictional Context

New York City in the 1700s was under **British colonial rule as part of New York Province** for virtually the entire century. The city originated as the Dutch colony of **New Amsterdam** (founded 1626) and was seized by the English in **1664**, renamed New York. A small Dutch reconquest briefly restored "New Orange" in 1673–74 before English rule was permanently restored. By 1700 the city was firmly British, though Dutch families and institutions — particularly the Dutch Reformed Church — remained socially dominant and continued generating Dutch-language records throughout the century.

**Critical implication:** There was **no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths** anywhere in New York during the 1700s. All vital events were recorded by churches — or not at all. Church records are therefore the primary and often *only* source for baptisms, marriages, and burials.

The first U.S. federal census was not taken until **1790**, and New York became a state only in **1788**. For the bulk of the 1700s, you are working within a colonial administrative structure: the **Prerogative Court** handled probate, the **Mayor's Court** handled civil matters, and the **New York Provincial Assembly** generated legislative and tax records.

> ⚠️ **Note on FamilySearch Wiki pages:** The wiki_place_page calls for New York (all four sections: home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and the constructed-URL wiki_read calls for New York Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, and Census pages all returned only a generic fallback page rather than New York-specific content. The specific claims below come from the `wiki_search` full-text results (which did return NYC-specific content with source URLs) and the `collections_search` / `volume_search` results. Visit [FamilySearch Wiki: New York City Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy) directly for additional up-to-date guidance.

---

## Record Types & Access

### 1. 🏛️ Church Records — **HIGHEST PRIORITY**

The single most important source class for 1700s NYC. No civil registration existed; churches recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials.

**FamilySearch Indexed Collection:**
- **New York, Church Records, 1640–1940** (Collection ID: 1469062)
  - 2,345,678 records, 1,172,839 images
  - **Access level: Indexed + images** (name-searchable)
  - [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)
  - Scope is the entire New York state — search broadly; city records are included

**FamilySearch Digitized Volume (NYC-specific):**
- **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, New York City, 1700–1776** (Image Group: 007733180)
  - 211 images, **0% name-indexed, NOT full-text searchable**
  - Language: **Dutch** ⚠️
  - **Access level: Browse-only** — must be paged through image by image with no search; requires ability to read 18th-century Dutch handwriting
  - This is the oldest continuous vital record series in the city, beginning 1639

**Key denominations with colonial-era NYC records** (per FamilySearch Wiki search result at [New York City Genealogy – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)):
| Denomination | Repository |
|---|---|
| Dutch Reformed | FamilySearch (volume above); New-York Historical Society; NYG&B |
| Anglican / Episcopalian (Trinity Church, founded 1698) | Trinity Church Archives; NYG&B; New-York Historical Society |
| Presbyterian | New-York Historical Society; NYG&B |
| Other (Quaker, Lutheran, Jewish) | Denomination archives; NYG&B |

---

### 2. 📜 Probate Records

**FamilySearch Indexed Collection:**
- **New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971** (Collection ID: 1542780)
  - 987,654 records, 493,827 images
  - **Access level: Indexed + images**
  - [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)

**Critical colonial quirk:** Wills in colonial New York were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** (not county-level courts). The **New-York Historical Society** published the *Abstracts of Wills* series, which provides a printed index to colonial probate. Search this series before assuming a will isn't indexed. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki – Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))

---

### 3. 🏡 Land Records

**FamilySearch Indexed Collection:**
- **New York, Land Records, 1630–1975** (Collection ID: 2078654)
  - 1,567,890 records, 783,945 images
  - **Access level: Indexed + images**
  - [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654)

Colonial land records include **patents** (crown grants), **deeds**, and **conveyances**. The NY State Archives holds the original **New York Colonial Manuscripts**, which include land-related administrative records. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki – Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

---

### 4. ⚖️ Court Records

The **Mayor's Court** was the principal civil court in colonial NYC. Records are held at the **New York State Archives** within the **New York Colonial Manuscripts** collection. FamilySearch's `volume_search` returned no digitized image volumes specific to court records for the 1700s — treat these as **physical/microfilm only**, requiring a visit to or correspondence with the State Archives.

---

### 5. 🪖 Military / Militia Records

Colonial New York Province maintained **militia rolls** listing men of military age — useful as a residence and age-indicator source. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki – Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))

- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) holds digitized military records, including some colonial-era material
- **National Archives (NARA)** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) holds federal-era military records (post-1776 Revolution)
- For pre-Revolutionary militia specifically, the **New York State Archives** is the primary repository

---

### 6. 💰 Tax Records

**Ward-level tax assessment lists** survive for some years in colonial NYC. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki – Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))

**FamilySearch Indexed Collection (borderline — starts 1799):**
- **New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804** (Collection ID: 1678432)
  - 123,456 records, 61,728 images — starts at the very end of the target period
  - [Search on FamilySearch](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432)

Pre-1799 ward tax lists are held physically at the **New York City Municipal Archives** and the **New York State Archives**; digitization coverage on FamilySearch is a gap for the 1700s.

---

### 7. 📊 Census Records

**No federal census** existed until **1790** (first enumeration). Colonial-era "censuses" are actually provincial enumeration lists or tax lists — not systematic household enumerations. The first proper census that includes NYC is **1790 U.S. Federal Census**, at the very tail of your research window. Check Ancestry.com ([ancestry.com/search/collections/census/](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) for the 1790 census.

---

### 8. 📰 Newspapers

The **New York Gazette** (1725 onwards) is the oldest colonial-era newspaper and published legal notices, ship arrivals, runaway notices, and death announcements — all genealogically relevant. **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) holds historical newspaper collections including early American papers.

---

### 9. ⚰️ Cemetery Records

**FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) indexes burial records and memorial transcriptions; colonial-era NYC churchyards (Trinity Church, Shearith Israel, etc.) have been transcribed by genealogical societies.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Church records, land, probate — indexed online | Free online |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B)** | Vast manuscript and microfilm collection; published the *Record* journal; colonial records | Membership / on-site |
| **New-York Historical Society** | *Abstracts of Wills* series; Dutch Reformed registers; manuscripts | On-site / some online |
| **New York State Archives** | NY Colonial Manuscripts; Mayor's Court; militia; provincial records | On-site / some digitized |
| **New York City Municipal Archives** | City-level administrative records, tax lists | On-site |
| **Trinity Church Archives** | Anglican/Episcopalian baptism, marriage, burial registers from 1698 | Contact directly |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal-era records post-1776; some colonial land patents | archives.gov / on-site |

---

## Digitization Level Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Church Records (statewide) | ✅ Indexed + images | Search Collection 1469062 |
| Dutch Reformed Church Registers (NYC, 1700–1776) | 🔍 Browse-only, Dutch language | Image Group 007733180; 211 images |
| Land Records | ✅ Indexed + images | Collection 2078654 |
| Probate Records | ✅ Indexed + images | Collection 1542780 |
| Tax Rolls (1799–1804) | ✅ Indexed + images | Collection 1678432; barely overlaps target window |
| Court Records (Mayor's Court) | ❌ Physical/microfilm only | NY State Archives |
| Militia Rolls | ❌ Physical/microfilm only | NY State Archives; Fold3 for later period |
| Pre-1799 Ward Tax Lists | ❌ Physical only | NYC Municipal Archives |
| Civil Vital Records | ❌ Did not exist | No civil registration in colonial era |

---

## Key Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No civil registration** in colonial NYC — churches are the only source for vital events; if your ancestor wasn't baptized/married/buried by a church that kept records, the event may be unrecoverable.
2. **Dutch Reformed Church registers (1700–1776)** on FamilySearch are entirely in Dutch and must be browsed image-by-image (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) — plan for Dutch-language research or engage a translator.
3. **Dutch families persisted** in the Dutch Reformed church well after the 1664 English conquest — don't assume English records simply because the period is "British colonial."
4. **FamilySearch collections are at New York State scope** — when searching FamilySearch, search "New York" not just "New York City"; city records are embedded in state-level collections.
5. **Colonial wills** were proved at the Prerogative Court, not county courts — use the NYG&B/New-York Historical Society *Abstracts of Wills* series as your index before searching elsewhere.
6. **Federal census begins only in 1790** — for most of the 1700s, tax lists and church records substitute for household enumeration.
7. **The FamilySearch Wiki's specific pages** for New York Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Probate Records, and the NYC Genealogy place pages returned generic content in this survey — visit [familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy) directly for the most current researcher guidance.

---

## Suggested Starting Points

1. **Search FamilySearch Collection 1469062** (New York Church Records, 1640–1940) for your ancestor's name — this is the easiest first step and covers multiple denominations.
2. **Browse Image Group 007733180** (Dutch Reformed registers, 1700–1776) if your family was Dutch Reformed — expect Dutch-language entries.
3. **Search FamilySearch Collection 1542780** (Probate Records) for any males who may have left wills; cross-reference with the *Abstracts of Wills* at the New-York Historical Society.
4. **Contact the NYG&B** — they specialize in exactly this period and hold published and manuscript materials not available online.
5. **Check the NY State Archives' Colonial Manuscripts** for court, land, and administrative records not yet digitized.

# Virginia — Revolutionary War Research Guide (1775–1783)
**Focus: Military Service & Wartime Activities**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Virginia was one of the thirteen original colonies and is among the best-documented colonial jurisdictions in North America, with county-level record-keeping running from the 1630s (Wikipedia). During 1775–1783, Virginia operated as an independent commonwealth. County court systems continued to function throughout the war, and state military administration was centered in Richmond.

> **⚠ Critical census gap.** The 1790 federal census for Virginia does not survive — it was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. **Personal property tax lists from 1782 onward are the primary population substitute** and are essential to any Revolutionary War–era Virginia research. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))

---

## 1. 🎖 Military Records — Primary Sources

### National Archives (NARA) — Washington, D.C. / archives.gov
The richest genealogical sources for Virginia's Revolutionary War soldiers are at NARA ([Virginia Military Records#Revolutionary_War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)):

| Record Type | NARA Record Group | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Continental Line service records & muster rolls | **RG 93** | Name, rank, unit, dates of service |
| Pension & bounty-land warrant application files | **RG 15** | Biographically rich — often include age, birthplace, family members, widow's testimony |

Pension files are frequently the single most genealogically valuable Revolutionary War record. Widows' pensions especially capture family detail unavailable elsewhere.

**Access:** Many pension files are digitized on **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/). Full applications can also be ordered from NARA directly.

### Virginia State Holdings
- **Virginia militia records** — held at the **Library of Virginia, Richmond** ([Virginia Military Records#Revolutionary_War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- **Virginia State Navy records** — published series, also cited in the FamilySearch Wiki ([same source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))

### FamilySearch — Indexed Collection
- **Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783** — collection ID [1945678](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) (name-searchable)

### FamilySearch — Digitized Volume (Browse-Only)
| Image Group | Coverage | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| **005301447** | Revolutionary War land bounty warrants, 1779–1800 | 341 | ⚠ **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be read image by image |

---

## 2. 🏡 Post-War Bounty Land Records

After the war, Virginia granted bounty lands in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** to its veterans — meaning the land grants are in Ohio, not Virginia. Warrant and survey records connecting veterans to their claims are held at the **Virginia State Library** ([Virginia Military Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)).

- Image group **005301447** (above) covers these warrants (1779–1800) — browse-only
- Don't overlook Ohio-side land records when tracing a veteran who accepted a grant

---

## 3. 📋 Tax Records — Critical Census Substitute

Since the 1790 Virginia census is lost, **personal property tax lists from 1782–1784** are the earliest post-war population enumeration and are indispensable for placing families ([Virginia Military Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)).

| FamilySearch Resource | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Collection [1456723](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) — Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850 | 1782–1850 | Name-indexed |
| Image group **005301449** — State enumerations / tax lists | 1782–1799 | **Full-text searchable** (87 images; 0% name-indexed via record search — use FamilySearch full-text search instead) |

---

## 4. 📜 Land Records

Land grants, deeds, and patents situate families geographically and often document relationships between neighbors — useful for identifying associates and kin.

- **Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900** — collection [1734285](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) — name-indexed, covers the target period

Post-war bounty-land warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library also connect veterans to specific land claims ([Virginia Military Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands)).

---

## 5. ⛪ Church Records

Virginia had **no statewide civil registration** during 1775–1783. The Anglican / Protestant Episcopal Church was the established church; Baptist and Presbyterian congregations were also active. Parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the only vital event records for this period.

- **Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929** — collection [1598230](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) — name-indexed, covers the target period

> The FamilySearch Wiki page [Virginia_Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Church_Records) did not return Virginia-specific content in this session — consult that page directly for denominational holdings detail.

---

## 6. ⚖️ County Court Records

Virginia county courts recorded deeds, wills, estate inventories, guardian bonds, and civil actions. Many order books survive for the war period and name family members in estate and guardianship proceedings.

| FamilySearch Resource | Coverage | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Collection [2134567](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) — Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920 | Statewide | Name-indexed |
| Image group **005301448** — Augusta County court order books, 1775–1795 | Augusta Co. | **Partially indexed — 61%** of images name-searchable; remainder browse-only |

Augusta County is one example volume returned by `volume_search` (total digitized volumes for this period and record type: 3). Additional county volumes may exist beyond what this survey captured.

---

## 7. 🗓 Vital Records

Virginia did not establish **statewide civil registration** during this period — the FamilySearch Wiki's Virginia-specific vital records pages did not resolve in this session. Consult [Virginia_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records) directly for registration-start dates. For 1775–1783, church registers and county records (marriage bonds, wills naming children) are your primary vital-event sources.

---

## 8. 📰 Wartime Documentary Sources

Newspapers carried militia muster notices, loyalist property seizures, and desertion notices that can name individuals. **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical newspaper collections covering this era.

---

## 9. Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Primary Holdings for 1775–1783 |
|---|---|
| **National Archives (NARA)** — archives.gov | Continental Army service records (RG 93), pension & bounty-land files (RG 15) |
| **Library of Virginia, Richmond** — lva.virginia.gov | Virginia militia records, county microfilm, state government records |
| **Virginia State Library** | Bounty-land warrant & survey records (Virginia Military District of Ohio) |
| **Fold3** — fold3.com | Digitized pension files and service records |
| **FamilySearch** — familysearch.org | 5 indexed collections + 3 digitized volumes (see tables above) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Additional Virginia record collections |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers |

---

## 10. Coverage Gaps & Quirks

- **1790 Virginia census is destroyed** — tax lists 1782–1784 (collection 1456723; image group 005301449) are the substitute; search these first to locate any family after the war
- **No statewide civil registration** in 1775–1783 — rely on church registers (collection 1598230) and county court records (collection 2134567)
- **Bounty-land warrant volume (005301447) is browse-only** — 341 images, no name index, no full-text search; plan time to read these page by page
- **Virginia Military District bounty lands are in Ohio** — trace veterans' post-war land records in Ohio as well as Virginia
- **Many Virginia county records were later destroyed in the Civil War** — for affected counties, the Library of Virginia may hold state-level substitutes
- **FamilySearch Wiki place pages** for Virginia (all four sections: home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only generic content in this session — consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records directly for deeper guidance

# 📍 Locality Research Guide
## New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana — Early 1800s (c. 1800–1840)

---

## Jurisdictional Overview

New Orleans sits at the heart of one of the most complex jurisdictional histories in North America. The city was founded by France in 1718, ceded to Spain in 1763 (effective 1769), briefly returned to France in 1800, then transferred to the United States via the Louisiana Purchase in 1803. Louisiana was organized as the Territory of Orleans (1804) and achieved statehood in 1812. The early 1800s therefore span the transition from Spanish colonial governance to U.S. territorial status to early statehood — and records reflect all three systems.

**Critically for researchers:** Louisiana operates on the **Napoleonic civil law tradition**, not English common law. This means:
- The jurisdiction is divided into **parishes**, not counties (Orleans Parish = New Orleans)
- Legal documentation flows through **notarial archives** rather than deed books
- Probate is called **succession**; guardianship is called **tutorship**
- These differences make Louisiana records structurally unlike those in any other U.S. state

**⚠️ Note on civil registration:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana vital records, church records, land records, and the Louisiana/New Orleans Genealogy pages were all unavailable through the wiki tool in this session (all redirected to a generic page). Registration dates below are drawn from wiki_search results. Louisiana did **not** have statewide civil vital registration during the early 1800s — Catholic sacramental registers are the primary substitute for birth, marriage, and death records throughout this period.

---

## The Disaster Landscape — What Was Lost and What Survived

New Orleans' archival record was shaped by a cascade of disasters:

| Event | Year | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| **Great New Orleans Fire** | 1788 | Destroyed ~856 buildings in the French Quarter; significant colonial record losses |
| **Second Great Fire** | 1794 | Destroyed ~212 more buildings; further archival damage |
| Yellow fever epidemics | Recurrent | Disrupted record-keeping; enormous mortality |
| Hurricanes and floods | Recurrent | Ongoing damage to physical repositories |

**Despite these losses, substantial records survive** — partly because Spanish colonial administrators maintained duplicates, partly because the notarial system kept records in private notary offices scattered across the city, and partly because the Catholic church maintained registers independently of civil authority. The 1788 fire, notably, occurred under Spanish rule, and the Cabildo (the Spanish colonial governing body) continued to function and generate records in the aftermath.

---

## Record Types: What Survives, Where It Is, and How to Access It

---

### 1. 🕍 Catholic Sacramental Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
**Primary vital records substitute — most important source for this period**

There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in New Orleans during the early 1800s. The Catholic Church was the only institution systematically recording these vital events.

- **St. Louis Cathedral** (the Cathedral-Basilica of Saint Louis, King of France) maintained baptism, marriage, and burial registers continuously from **1731 to the present**, though with gaps due to the 1788 and 1794 fires. These are the single most important survival for early New Orleans families.
  ([FamilySearch Wiki — New Orleans Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))
- Other Catholic parish churches in New Orleans and surrounding areas also maintained registers.
- The **Archdiocese of New Orleans** holds the original registers; many have been microfilmed by FamilySearch.
  ([FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Church_Records#Catholic))

**Language warning:** Records are in **French** for the French colonial period (1718–1769), **Spanish** for the Spanish colonial period (1769–1803), and transitioning to **English** after 1803. Early 1800s registers often mix French and English. Researchers must be able to read the original language or obtain a translation.

**FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) — this indexed collection (Collection ID 1612905) covers the full target period and is the primary digital access point. Search this first.

**Digitization level:** Indexed + images (via the collection above). The Archdiocese also holds originals and microfilm.

---

### 2. 📜 Notarial Acts — The Heart of New Orleans Records
**Most comprehensive surviving civil record series**

Louisiana's civil law system routed nearly all significant legal transactions through notaries: property sales, marriage contracts, successions (probate), tutorships (guardianship), emancipations, slave transactions, commercial agreements, and more. Because records were held in private notary offices scattered across the city, many survived the 1788 and 1794 fires that destroyed centralized government archives.

- **The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over **30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734** — one of the largest collections of its kind in the United States.
  ([FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Notarial_Archives))
- **Colonial-era notarial records (French 1718–1769, Spanish 1769–1803)** are held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in the Old U.S. Mint building in New Orleans.
- Records from 1803 onward are at the Notarial Archives Research Center.

**Critical access quirk:** Notarial records are organized **by notary name and date**, not by party name. To use them effectively, you need an approximate date and the name of the notary. Published indexes and finding aids exist for some periods; the Notarial Archives Research Center staff can assist.

**FamilySearch digitized volume:** FamilySearch holds **1 digitized volume** of Orleans Parish notarial acts:
- Image Group `004990115` — 167 images, covering **1803–1820**, described as "Notarial Acts (surviving microfilm copies)"
- **Digitization level: Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be read image by image. Languages: French and English.

This is the only FamilySearch-digitized volume returned by volume_search for New Orleans in this period. The full notarial record series is far larger and exists primarily in physical form at the repositories above.

---

### 3. ⚖️ Probate Records (Successions)
**Excellent substitute for vital information**

Louisiana succession records (probate) are a treasure trove: they name the deceased, list heirs by name and relationship, inventory property (including enslaved people by name), and often document marriages and family connections. These frequently survive even when vital records do not.

**FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) — Collection ID 2078341, covers the full early 1800s window. Held at the Louisiana State Archives and parish courthouses.

**Also access through:** The Notarial Archives (succession proceedings went through notaries) and the Orleans Parish Civil District Court.

---

### 4. 👪 Census Records

| Census Year | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1810 | Territory of Orleans / Louisiana | Covers New Orleans |
| 1820 | Louisiana | Covers New Orleans |
| 1830 | Louisiana | Covers New Orleans |
| 1840 | Louisiana | Covers New Orleans |

Federal censuses from 1810 onward are available for New Orleans through Ancestry.com, FamilySearch, and other providers. These are name-indexed and searchable online.

**Territorial-era censuses (pre-1810):** Spanish colonial censuses (*padrones*) exist for some years and are held at the Louisiana Historical Center. These predate U.S. administration and are in Spanish.

**Mortality schedules** begin with the 1850 census and fall outside the early 1800s window.

---

### 5. ⛵ Immigration and Passenger Records
**New Orleans was the second-largest port of entry in the U.S.**

The city was a primary arrival point for immigrants throughout the early 1800s — Irish, German, French, Haitian refugees (post-1791 revolution), and enslaved people transported via the domestic slave trade.

- **NARA passenger lists** for New Orleans begin in 1820 and are available indexed at Ancestry.com and on microfilm at NARA's Southeast Region facility (Atlanta).
- Pre-1820 arrivals are documented sporadically in customs records and Spanish colonial records.
- **Haitian refugees (1791–1809):** A large wave of French Creole refugees from Saint-Domingue arrived, some via Cuba. Their records may appear in both New Orleans and earlier Cuban/Haitian records.
- **Military records** (War of 1812, Battle of New Orleans 1815): Service records and pension files at NARA (Fold3 and Ancestry.com) document many men present in New Orleans during this period.

---

### 6. 🏛️ Spanish Colonial Records (Cabildo / Government Records)
**Surviving records of the colonial governing body**

Records generated by the Cabildo (Spanish colonial town council) and by Spanish colonial courts survived partly because Spain maintained duplicate copies. These include court proceedings, property records, census-like enumerations, and administrative correspondence.

- Held at the **Louisiana Historical Center** in New Orleans and the **Louisiana State Archives** in Baton Rouge.
- The Louisiana State Archives holds territorial and early statehood records (post-1803).
  ([FamilySearch Wiki — Louisiana Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#Parish_System))

---

### 7. 🏡 Land Records

Louisiana land titles derive from grants made under French, Spanish, and U.S. authority — all three systems are relevant for early 1800s families.

- **Spanish land grants** (pre-1803): Louisiana Historical Center and the U.S. General Land Office (Bureau of Land Management GLO Records site, glorecords.blm.gov)
- **U.S.-era land patents** (post-1803): BLM GLO Records website (glorecords.blm.gov) — searchable online
- **Notarial records** document property sales and transfers throughout the period (see §2 above)

**Note:** Because Louisiana was a federal land state (public land state), original land patents from the U.S. period are at the BLM GLO site, not at a state land office.

---

### 8. 📰 Newspapers

New Orleans had an active press in the early 1800s. Newspapers published vital notices (births, marriages, deaths), legal notices (successions, land sales, runaway slave advertisements), and ship arrivals.

- **Newspapers.com** and the **Library of Congress Chronicling America** project hold digitized runs of early New Orleans papers, including the *Louisiana Gazette* and *L'Ami des Lois*.
- The **Louisiana State Library** and **Tulane University** hold physical collections.

---

### 9. 🔗 People of Color: Free and Enslaved

New Orleans in the early 1800s had one of the largest communities of **free people of color** (*gens de couleur libres*) in the United States. Enslaved people also appear in records in significant ways.

- **St. Louis Cathedral registers** recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials for free and enslaved persons of color — these registers are sometimes segregated by status or race, sometimes integrated.
- **Notarial acts** document emancipations (freedom papers), sales, and other transactions involving enslaved people, often recording names, ages, origins, and skills.
- **Succession inventories** name enslaved people.
- **The FamilySearch collection** [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) includes sacramental records covering these communities.
- Specialized databases: the **Louisiana Slave Database** (Tulane University) and **Afro-Louisiana History and Genealogy** database (compiled by Gwendolyn Midlo Hall) index enslaved people named in notarial and other records.

---

## Substitute Source Strategy (When Primary Records Are Missing)

| If you cannot find… | Try instead… |
|---|---|
| Birth record | St. Louis Cathedral baptismal register; godparent records in same registers |
| Marriage record | Cathedral marriage register; notarial marriage contract; succession naming spouse |
| Death record | Cathedral burial register; succession/probate record; newspaper notice |
| Property deed | Notarial act (sale/transfer); succession inventory; U.S.-era BLM patent |
| Census for pre-1810 | Spanish colonial census (*padrón*) at Louisiana Historical Center |
| Destroyed colonial record | Check for Spanish duplicate copies at Louisiana Historical Center |
| Identity of free person of color | Cathedral register (often records race/status); notarial emancipation act |

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | 30M+ pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; some digital indexes |
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint) | French/Spanish colonial records, pre-1803 notarial acts, *padrones* | In-person |
| **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge) | Territorial and early statehood records (post-1803) | In-person; some online |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans** | Original Catholic sacramental registers | In-person; microfilm at FamilySearch |
| **FamilySearch** | Church Records 1718–1925 (indexed); 1 notarial volume (browse-only) | Online free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census (1810–1840); passenger lists (1820+); military records | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records (War of 1812, pension files) | Subscription |
| **NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta)** | Federal records, passenger lists, naturalization | In-person / microfilm |
| **Tulane University / Historic New Orleans Collection** | Newspapers, manuscript collections, specialized databases | In-person |

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 | [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) | 1718–1925 | Indexed + images |
| Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 | [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) | 1756–1984 | Indexed + images |
| Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 | [1543892](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1543892) | 1819–1964 | Index only (no images) |
| Orleans Parish Notarial Acts (microfilm) | DGS `004990115` | 1803–1820 | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text; French & English |
| Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957 | [1798054](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1798054) | 1837–1957 | Post-period; background context |

---

## Key Quirks for New Orleans Research

1. **"Parish" means two different things in Louisiana.** A Louisiana civil *parish* (like Orleans Parish) is equivalent to a county elsewhere. A Catholic *parish* (like St. Louis Cathedral parish) is a church congregation. Records labelled "parish records" may be either type — always determine which before searching.
2. **Language shifts mid-record.** Registers transition from Spanish to French to English across the early 1800s; a single register may contain all three languages. Be prepared to read all three or seek a translator.
3. **The 1788 and 1794 fires created gaps, not a total loss.** Many records survive with gaps; do not assume a record is gone because it isn't indexed — browse originals and check for duplicates in Spanish colonial holdings.
4. **Notarial records require knowing the notary.** Without an approximate date and notary name, these records are difficult to navigate. Published name indexes and the Notarial Archives Research Center staff are essential entry points.
5. **No civil vital registration in Louisiana during the early 1800s.** Louisiana did not require statewide registration of births, marriages, or deaths during this period. Catholic church registers are the primary substitute.
6. **The Feliciana Parish split (1824)** divided Feliciana Parish into East and West Feliciana Parish. If your ancestors were in Feliciana (north of Baton Rouge), records could be under either successor parish depending on where within the original territory the event occurred — search both.
7. **New Orleans was a major port.** If an ancestor arrived in the early 1800s, check New Orleans passenger lists (Ancestry, NARA) for arrival evidence before looking for in-state records.
8. **Free people of color had distinct legal status** documented in notarial records, sacramental registers (often with racial/status notation), and emancipation acts — all of which survive and are searchable.

- External links for New Orleans specifically in 1790–1850 were generic (Ancestry census, NARA, Find A Grave, Fold3, Newspapers.com) — no time-windowed Louisiana-specific curated external links were returned.

---

This is an extraordinarily rich research environment despite the disaster losses — the survival of the notarial archives alone makes New Orleans families traceable far deeper than most early American jurisdictions. The **St. Louis Cathedral registers** and the **Notarial Archives** are your twin pillars; the **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** FamilySearch collection is the place to start online.

Here is your locality research guide for Port of Boston immigration arrivals, 1840s.

---

# Port of Boston, Massachusetts — Immigration Records Guide (1840s)

## Jurisdictional Context

**Boston, Suffolk County, Massachusetts, United States** (standardPlace: *Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States*). Boston was a federally supervised customs port throughout the 1840s, with no boundary or jurisdictional changes affecting the port during this period. It was one of the five major U.S. ports of entry during the decade and received particularly large waves of Irish famine emigrants after 1845; by 1850 more than a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born, per Wikipedia. Records were created at three overlapping levels: **federal** (customs/passenger lists, federal courts), **state** (Massachusetts courts, town registers), and **local church** (denominational registers).

---

## Record Types, Access, and Repositories

### 1. 🚢 Customs Passenger Lists — PRIMARY SOURCE
**Coverage:** Port of Boston, 1840–1891 (federal law since 1819 required ship captains to file passenger manifests with the customs collector at each port)

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch collection | *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* — [Collection 1784312](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) |
| Digitized volume found | Image Group **003345210** — 389 images covering 1840–1850, Port of Boston |
| **Access level** | ⚠️ **Full-text searchable, NOT name-indexed** — recordSearchablePercent = 3%; fulltextSearchable = true. Use FamilySearch full-text search before resorting to page-by-page browsing. |
| Typical 1840s content | Name, age, sex, occupation, country of origin — **not town of origin**. Exact village of birth usually absent; work backward from Irish/German records to supply it. |
| Originals | National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA) — **NARA Record Group 36** |
| Also indexed on | Ancestry.com |

> ⚠️ **Key quirk:** 1840s manifests record *country* of origin, not village. For Irish immigrants, you will likely need church or civil records in Ireland to identify the specific townland or parish of origin.

The FamilySearch Wiki search confirmed that these lists are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry and that the National Archives at Boston (Waltham) holds the originals. ([Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Immigration, "Port of Boston"](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston))

---

### 2. 📜 Naturalization Records — ESSENTIAL FOLLOW-ON
**Coverage:** Pre-1906, any court of record (federal, state, or local) could naturalize immigrants — records are **scattered across multiple repositories**.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch collection | *Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906* — [Collection 1459213](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) |
| Boston-area courts | U.S. Circuit Court; U.S. District Court; Suffolk County Court of Common Pleas; Suffolk County Superior Court |
| Record types | Declaration of Intention ("First Papers") + Petition for Naturalization — these were often filed years apart in *different* courts; search all of them |
| Originals | NARA Waltham (federal court records); Massachusetts State Archives (state court records) |

> ⚠️ **Key quirk:** A man who declared his intention in Boston in 1843 may not have completed naturalization until the 1850s, potentially in a different county or state if he moved. First Papers and Final Papers may be in entirely different repositories.

---

### 3. ⛪ Church Records — VITAL FOR TRACKING ARRIVALS BEFORE CIVIL REGISTRATION
Catholic, Protestant, and other denominational registers are often the only source for vital events in the 1840s, especially for Irish Catholic and German immigrants.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch collection | *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* — [Collection 1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) |
| Key Catholic parishes | Cathedral of the Holy Cross; St. Patrick's (both confirmed in FamilySearch Wiki search results) |
| Repository for Catholic registers | **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** (confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki search) |
| Content | Baptisms, marriages, burials — often recording Irish townland or county of origin, which passenger lists omit |

> ⚠️ **Registration gap note:** The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Massachusetts Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — the specific statewide civil registration start date for Massachusetts could not be confirmed from a tool-returned URL. Consult the [FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records) page directly for registration dates by level (town vs. state). Church registers are the recommended substitute for vital events in this decade regardless.

---

### 4. 📋 Town Vital Records

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch collection | *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* — [Collection 2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) |
| Note | Massachusetts towns registered vital events locally before statewide registration; Boston's town/city records in this series may document immigrant children born in Boston shortly after arrival |

---

### 5. 📰 The Pilot "Missing Persons" Advertisements — UNIQUE IMMIGRANT RESOURCE
Boston's Irish Catholic newspaper *The Pilot* published **arrival notices** and **missing-persons advertisements** placed by immigrants seeking relatives who had emigrated before them. This is one of the most genealogically distinctive sources for 1840s Boston Irish arrivals. (Confirmed by Wikipedia result.)

| Access | Detail |
|---|---|
| Database | *The Pilot* Missing Persons database — searchable online; hosted by Boston College |
| Historical newspapers broadly | Newspapers.com (returned by external_links_search) |

---

### 6. 👪 Federal Census Records — 1840 & 1850

| Census | Detail |
|---|---|
| 1840 | Names only the head of household; counts other members by age/sex brackets — useful to confirm a family's presence in Boston |
| **1850** | **First census to name every household member** — search this as the immediate post-arrival snapshot; age, birthplace (country), and real estate listed |
| Access | Ancestry.com ([census collection](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/), returned by external_links_search) |

---

### 7. ⚖️ Probate Records

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| FamilySearch collection | *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* — [Collection 1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) |
| Relevance | Wills and estate inventories may name kin still in Ireland/Germany or elsewhere in the U.S., providing clues to origin and extended family |
| Repository | Suffolk County Probate Court; Massachusetts State Archives |

---

### 8. 🪖 Military Records
Some 1840s immigrants subsequently served in the Mexican-American War (1846–48) or are found in later Civil War records.

| Access | Fold3 (returned by external_links_search) — service records, pension files |
|---|---|
| National Archives | NARA (returned by external_links_search) — [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |

---

### 9. ⚰️ Cemetery Records

| Access | Find A Grave (returned by external_links_search) — [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) |
|---|---|
| Note | Boston's early immigrant cemeteries (e.g., Holy Cross Cemetery in Malden) hold mid-19th-century Catholic burials |

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's Held | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston (Waltham, MA)** | Original customs passenger lists (RG 36); federal court naturalization records | In-person; microfilm/digital via FamilySearch/Ancestry |
| **FamilySearch** | Passenger lists collection 1784312; naturalization collection 1459213; church records 1921657; town vitals 2061550; probate 1678901 | Free online at familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Indexed passenger lists; federal census; naturalization records | Subscription |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Irish immigrants, 1840s onward | Contact archives directly |
| **Massachusetts State Archives** (Boston) | State court naturalization records; Massachusetts vital records | In-person and some online |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** | New England genealogical collections, compiled databases, *The Pilot* materials | Membership/subscription; americanancestors.org |
| **Boston Public Library** | Historical newspapers; city directories; local histories | In-person and some digital |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | Digitization Level |
|---|---|
| Passenger Lists, 1840–1850 (vol. 003345210) | ⚠️ Full-text searchable; only 3% name-indexed — search by full-text before browsing |
| Massachusetts Passenger Lists collection (1784312) | Indexed collection on FamilySearch |
| Massachusetts Naturalization Records (1459213) | Indexed collection on FamilySearch |
| Massachusetts Church Records (1921657) | Indexed collection on FamilySearch |
| Massachusetts Town Vital Records (2061550) | Indexed collection on FamilySearch |
| Massachusetts Probate Records (1678901) | Indexed collection on FamilySearch |
| Federal court naturalization originals | Physical at NARA Waltham; some microfilmed |
| Catholic parish registers (Archdiocese) | Largely physical — contact archives |

---

## Research Quirks & Warnings

1. **Country, not village, on passenger lists.** 1840s manifests record country of origin. Pin down the Irish townland or German village by working backward from church records, later naturalization papers, or the 1880 U.S. census (which adds parents' birthplaces).
2. **Full-text search first.** The Port of Boston 1840–1850 digitized volume (003345210) is 3% name-indexed but full-text searchable — run a full-text search before browsing 389 images page by page.
3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered.** Declaration of Intention and Petition for Naturalization may be in different courts and different years. Search federal *and* state/local courts.
4. **Don't skip church records.** For Irish Catholic arrivals especially, parish registers often supply the Irish county or parish that no other American record provides.
5. **Check *The Pilot* database.** Tens of thousands of missing-persons notices were published; it is a searchable, free resource unique to the Boston Irish research community.
6. **Wiki gaps noted.** The FamilySearch Wiki place-pages for Massachusetts and the specific Massachusetts Vital Records, Immigration, and Naturalization pages returned only generic content during this survey. For the most current guidance on those topics, consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly: [Massachusetts Immigration](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration) and [Massachusetts Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records).

---

# Locality Research Guide
## Native American Families in Oklahoma / Indian Territory, Mid-1800s (c. 1830–1900)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

The area that became Oklahoma was, throughout the mid-1800s, **Indian Territory** — not yet a U.S. state. The Indian Removal Act of 1830 compelled the relocation of the **Five Civilized Tribes** (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, and Seminole) from the southeastern U.S. via the Trail of Tears. The 1834 Indian Intercourse Act formally designated the region as Indian Territory under federal oversight.

Critically for research: **no civil county court infrastructure existed** in Indian Territory during this period. Families were not recorded through courthouse deed books or county vital registers — they appear instead through federal tribal enrollment rolls, Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) agency records, tribal government records, treaty schedules, and missionary registers. Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until **1907**, and county-level civil records only begin in earnest from around 1890 onward in the western Oklahoma Territory half.

A two-territory split occurred in 1890: **Oklahoma Territory** (western, opened by Land Run in 1889) in the west, with county infrastructure developing; **Indian Territory** (eastern, tribal nations) in the east. From 1830 to 1890, the entire region was Indian Territory. Research for the mid-1800s belongs almost entirely in the Indian Territory framework.

---

### Record Coverage Summary

**FamilySearch Collections Search** (scope: Oklahoma) returned 4 indexed collections covering the target period:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907 | 1834–1907 | 234,567 | 117,283 | Indexed + images |
| **Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** | 1851–1959 | 567,890 | 283,945 | Indexed + images |
| Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965 | 1820–1965 | 123,456 | 61,728 | Indexed + images |
| Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995 | 1890–1995 | 456,789 | 228,394 | Indexed (post-period) |

The Indian Censuses and Rolls collection and the Mission and Church Records collection are the primary FamilySearch starting points for the mid-1800s target window.

**FamilySearch Digitized Volumes** (volume search) returned **1 volume** specifically classified as Indigenous records for Indian Territory:

| Image Group | Images | Name-Indexed | Full-Text | Record Type | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 002298871 | 940 | 99% | Yes | Tribal Enrollment Cards | Indian Territory, 1840–1870 |

This volume is the highest-access digitized source confirmed for the core target window: name-searchable, full-text searchable, and covers the heart of the mid-1800s period.

> ⚠️ **Coverage gap:** `volume_search` returned a total of 1 result. Additional volumes may exist under different place names (e.g., individual tribal nation names, "Cherokee Nation," "Choctaw Nation") — search those separately. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma and Indian Territory returned only generic content (not Oklahoma-specific articles), which is a gap in the online guidance layer; consult FamilySearch directly at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records).

---

### Record Types — Ranked by Priority for Mid-1800s Research

#### 1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls ⭐ *Primary source class*

The FamilySearch Wiki confirms the following pre-Dawes rolls for the mid-1800s window ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls)):

| Roll | Tribe | Year | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Old Settler Cherokee Roll | Cherokee | 1851 | Lists Cherokees who removed before forced relocation |
| Drennen Roll | Cherokee | 1852 | Post-removal census |
| Henderson Roll | Cherokee | 1835 | Pre-Trail of Tears |
| Armstrong Roll | Choctaw | 1831 | Early removal roll |
| Ward Roll | Choctaw | 1851 | Census roll |
| Parsons & Abbott Roll | Creek/Muscogee | 1832 | |
| Duval Roll | Creek/Muscogee | 1857 | |
| Mullay Roll | Chickasaw | 1851 | |

Each roll typically records the head of household, family members, ages, sex, and sometimes blood quantum. Many list freedmen (formerly enslaved persons) separately.

**The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** are the most comprehensive enrollment, listing name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation for the Five Civilized Tribes. Though they postdate your target period, they are indispensable for working backward to mid-1800s ancestors. Indexed at FamilySearch ([collection 1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)) and Ancestry. Physical originals held at **NARA – Fort Worth** (see below).

#### 2. Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records ⭐

The BIA maintained records through its agencies stationed in Indian Territory. Confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)):

- **Annuity payment rolls** — list household members eligible for treaty-stipulated payments; extremely useful for mid-1800s family reconstruction
- **Agency correspondence files** — name individuals in disputes, removals, land claims, and welfare matters
- **School and mission school records** — enrollment registers, often naming parents
- **Census schedules** — the BIA conducted its own periodic tribal censuses separate from the federal decennial census

**Held at:** NARA – Fort Worth, Texas (primary repository for Five Civilized Tribes records) and NARA – Washington, D.C. (Record Group 75, Bureau of Indian Affairs). Some records are microfilmed and available via FamilySearch.

#### 3. Missionary and Church Records

Confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki ([source](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Missionary_Records)): Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries operated among the relocated tribes from the 1820s onward and kept:

- Registers of converts (baptisms)
- Marriage registers
- School enrollment lists
- Death/burial registers
- Community rolls of congregation members

FamilySearch's **Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965** (collection [1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)) — 123,456 records, 61,728 images — is the indexed access point. Physical originals may be held at denominational archives (American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society, United Methodist Archives Center) and the **Oklahoma Historical Society**.

#### 4. Treaty Records and Federal Documents

Treaties between the U.S. government and individual tribes — signed throughout the 1830s–1860s — often include schedules naming tribal members, clan structures, and property holdings. Key treaties include:

- Treaty of New Echota (1835) — Cherokee removal
- Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek (1830) — Choctaw removal
- Treaty of Payne's Landing (1832) — Seminole removal

**Held at:** NARA – Washington, D.C. (Record Group 75); published in Charles J. Kappler's *Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties* (digitized and searchable at [digital.library.okstate.edu](https://digital.library.okstate.edu/kappler/)).

#### 5. Land and Allotment Records

FamilySearch's **Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907** (collection [1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images — covers the transition from communal tribal landholding to individual allotments. The Dawes Act (1887) and Curtis Act (1898) drove the allotment era, so most allotment records postdate the mid-1800s core target; however, **pre-allotment tribal land permit records** exist from earlier decades.

The **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO)** records cover the Oklahoma Land Runs of 1889 onward. For tribal land before allotment, work through the BIA and tribal national archives.

#### 6. U.S. Federal Census — Special Indian Schedules

The standard federal decennial censuses (1860, 1870, 1880, 1890, 1900) largely did not enumerate Indian Territory residents in the main population schedules. However:

- **Special Indian Census Schedules** were conducted by the BIA (not Census Bureau) — these sometimes survive in NARA Record Group 75
- The **1900 federal census** does include Indian Territory as a separate schedule
- Mortality schedules (1850–1885) may capture deaths among tribal members in contact zones

FamilySearch's Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959 (collection [1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)) likely includes these special schedules alongside the enrollment rolls.

#### 7. Military Records

- Several tribes maintained their own militias and had service records
- U.S. Army maintained posts throughout Indian Territory (Fort Gibson, Fort Washita, Fort Arbuckle, Fort Cobb); post returns and correspondence name local individuals
- **Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek, and Chickasaw** regiments served in the Civil War (on both sides) — Confederate service records and pension files survive; Confederate pension applications filed with Oklahoma after statehood name family members
- **Fold3.com** and NARA hold federal military records; the **Oklahoma Historical Society** holds Confederate Oklahoma pension files

#### 8. Vital Records — Significant Gap

Oklahoma did not establish statewide civil vital registration until **1908** (the year after statehood). For the mid-1800s, there are **no civil birth, marriage, or death records**. Family vital events must be reconstructed from the record classes above (tribal rolls, church registers, BIA records). This is a critical gap — be explicit in research plans that standard vital records do not exist for this period.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA – Fort Worth, TX** | Dawes Rolls, Five Civilized Tribes allotment jackets, BIA agency records | In-person and microfilm; some digitized at FamilySearch/Ancestry |
| **NARA – Washington, D.C.** | Record Group 75 (BIA), treaty records, early agency correspondence | In-person; some online |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society (OHS)** | Territorial records, tribal newspapers (*Cherokee Phoenix*, *Cherokee Advocate*), Civil War pension files, oral history collections | In-person (OKC); some online at [gateway.okhistory.org](https://gateway.okhistory.org) |
| **Cherokee Nation Cultural Resource Center** | Cherokee tribal records, citizenship records, tribal rolls | Contact tribal offices directly |
| **Five Civilized Tribes Museum (Muskogee)** | Artifacts and some archival materials for all five tribes | In-person |
| **Western History Collections, Univ. of Oklahoma** | Manuscript collections, BIA records, Indian Territory maps | In-person |
| **FamilySearch (online)** | Indexed rolls and images (collections noted above) | Free at familysearch.org |
| **Ancestry.com** | Dawes Rolls, some BIA annuity rolls, federal census | Subscription |

---

### External Resources Confirmed

FamilySearch's curated external links for this place and period returned 6 resources (though the place-filter may have returned these generically rather than Oklahoma-specifically):

- **National Archives (archives.gov)** — primary repository for BIA Record Group 75
- **Ancestry.com** — U.S. Federal Census Collection and Dawes Rolls
- **Fold3.com** — Military records
- **Find A Grave (findagrave.com)** — Cemetery records (limited for mid-1800s Indian Territory)
- **Newspapers.com** — Historical newspapers (tribal newspapers like *Cherokee Phoenix* digitized separately at OHS)
- **FamilySearch Wiki** — Vital Records category

---

### Research Quirks and Cautions

1. **No county-level records exist for mid-1800s Indian Territory.** Do not search county courthouses or expect deed books, probate files, or court records from this era — the tribal national governments and BIA held that authority.

2. **Tribal rolls are organized by tribe, then band or district, not alphabetically by surname.** Know which tribe you are researching before searching a roll.

3. **Freedmen rolls are separate.** Persons formerly enslaved by tribal members were enrolled on separate "Freedmen" rolls in the Dawes series and in earlier rolls — they have the same legal access to tribal citizenship research but appear in different sections.

4. **Blood quantum and "full-blood" vs. "mixed-blood" designations** appear on rolls and reflect federal classification, not necessarily cultural identity or the family's own understanding. These designations affect which roll a person appears on.

5. **Many mid-1800s rolls were recorded in English by non-tribal recorders**, sometimes phonetically rendering Native names — search for spelling variants and anglicized name equivalents.

6. **The Civil War disrupted Indian Territory records severely** — tribal archives were damaged or lost, some census records burned, and families scattered. The period 1861–1865 is a particular gap; reconstruct around it using pre-war and post-war rolls.

7. **Tribal newspapers** (*Cherokee Phoenix*, *Cherokee Advocate*, *Choctaw Telegraph*) published notices, legal announcements, and community news that name individuals — held at OHS and partially digitized.

8. **FamilySearch wiki pages for Oklahoma and Indian Territory returned generic content** in this survey — consult the FamilySearch Research Wiki directly at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma) and [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records) for additional strategy detail not captured here.

---

### Suggested Research Sequence

1. **Identify the tribe** — you must know which of the Five Civilized Tribes (or other group) your ancestor belonged to before rolls or BIA records can be effectively searched.
2. **Start with the Dawes Rolls** (1898–1914) on FamilySearch collection [1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) or Ancestry — use Dawes as a confirmed anchor, then work backward through the pre-Dawes mid-1800s rolls listed above.
3. **Search the FamilySearch Tribal Enrollment Cards volume** (image group 002298871, 940 images, 99% name-indexed, full-text searchable) — directly targets the 1840–1870 window.
4. **Request the allotment jacket** from NARA Fort Worth — these files contain the full enrollment record, interview transcripts, birth affidavits, and family testimony, often reaching back decades.
5. **Search BIA annuity rolls at NARA** (RG 75) for the relevant tribe and agency — these are the richest mid-1800s family sources.
6. **Search missionary registers** via FamilySearch collection [1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321) for the relevant denomination.
7. **Check tribal newspapers and OHS holdings** for community-level documentation.

## Pennsylvania Quaker Community Records — Late 1700s
**Locality Guide** | Place: Pennsylvania, United States | Period: c. 1750–1800

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania became a state in 1787. For the late 1700s, records were generated under both colonial governance (pre-1776) and early statehood (post-1787). **No statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths existed in this period** — Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide vital registration until 1906 (FamilySearch Wiki via wiki_search). Quaker meeting records therefore function as the **primary substitute for civil vital records** for Friends families throughout this entire era.

Quaker communities were concentrated in **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties** (Wikipedia: *Quakers in Pennsylvania*).

---

### ⭐ The Core Resource: Quaker Meeting Records

This is where your research must begin and center. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)), monthly meeting records are among the most detailed religious records in Pennsylvania and routinely contain:

| Record Type | What It Documents |
|---|---|
| **Monthly meeting minutes** | Births, marriages, deaths |
| **Certificates of removal** | Membership transfers between meetings — essential for tracking migration |
| **Disownments** | Disciplinary proceedings naming the individual and reason (also catches Revolutionary War-era service, as Quakers who enlisted were typically disowned) |
| **Marriage certificates** | Signed by **all attendees** — can name dozens of relatives and witnesses at once |

#### Meeting Structure
- **Monthly meeting** — the basic record-creating unit; where you'll find the most genealogical detail
- **Quarterly meeting** — supervises monthly meetings
- **Yearly meeting** — Philadelphia Yearly Meeting was the governing body for most Pennsylvania Friends

#### Primary Repositories

1. **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** *(Swarthmore, PA)* — holds the largest collection of American Quaker records in the country (FamilySearch Wiki; Wikipedia)
2. **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** *(Haverford, PA)* — a major manuscript repository for Pennsylvania Friends records (Wikipedia)

Both institutions hold original manuscript meeting minutes, registers, and certificates that have not been fully digitized and must be consulted in person or by correspondence.

#### Published Finding Aid — Start Here

**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*** (6 volumes) abstracts meeting records from Pennsylvania and other states. This is the standard published index to Quaker genealogical records and should be your first search before going to manuscript sources. FamilySearch has also microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers ([Pennsylvania Church Records — Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)).

---

### FamilySearch Digitized Volumes (Religious / Church Records, 1700–1810)

`volume_search` returned **1 digitized volume** for Pennsylvania religious records in this window (totalResults: 1):

| Volume | Image Group | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800 | 001188322 | 145 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable |

This volume must be viewed image by image with no search capability. It covers the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting's overarching minutes — useful for understanding disciplinary actions and structural decisions, but individual birth/marriage/death entries will be in the monthly meeting registers, most of which are **not yet digitized on FamilySearch** and remain on microfilm or in physical repositories.

---

### FamilySearch Collections Overlapping 1750–1800

`collections_search` returned the following Pennsylvania collections relevant to this period:

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Records | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 | [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | **Index only — no images** |

These are not Quaker-specific but will include Friends who appeared in civil and legal contexts (wills, estate administration, marriage bonds).

---

### Vital Records — No Civil Registration Existed

Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** of births, marriages, or deaths during the late 1700s. For Quaker families, the meeting records described above are the complete substitute. Non-Quaker neighbors may appear in county court marriage bonds or church registers of other denominations, but for Friends, look exclusively to the meeting.

---

### Census Records

The first federal census (1790) falls within the late 1700s and will enumerate Pennsylvania Quaker households. It lists only heads of household with counts for other members. Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Mortality schedules did not begin until 1850.

---

### Land and Probate Records

- **FamilySearch — Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection 1999196): 893,214 indexed records. Quakers used the standard colonial and state court systems for wills and estate administration.
- **County deed books** at county courthouses and the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) record land transactions and may name family members in conveyances.
- Tax lists (county-level) also survive for much of the late 1700s and can help locate individuals between censuses.

---

### Military Records — A Special Quaker Consideration

Quakers were committed pacifists. In the Revolutionary War era:
- Friends who **enlisted were disowned** — making disownment records in the monthly meeting minutes the record to find
- Friends who **refused service** may appear in exemption lists or local militia records
- For any who did serve, Revolutionary War service records and pension files are at **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) and on **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/))

---

### Cemetery Records

Quaker meetings maintained their own burial grounds, often adjacent to the meetinghouse. Deaths were recorded in monthly meeting minutes. **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) indexes some Quaker burial grounds but coverage for 1750–1800 is sparse and should be treated as supplementary only.

---

### Newspapers

Historical Pennsylvania newspapers are available on **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)). Pre-1800 coverage is limited but may include estate advertisements, legal notices, and land sale announcements.

---

### Gaps and Caveats

| Gap | Detail |
|---|---|
| **FamilySearch Wiki pages** | The Pennsylvania-specific wiki pages (Church Records, Vital Records, state Genealogy overview) returned generic content rather than Pennsylvania-specific articles — consult the wiki directly at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records) |
| **Digitized meeting records** | Only 1 FamilySearch volume (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes) was found for religious records in this period. Most individual monthly meeting registers exist on **microfilm** only and must be browsed or ordered through FamilySearch or consulted at Swarthmore/Haverford |
| **External links** | The curated external-links search returned only generic repositories (Ancestry census, NARA, FindAGrave, Fold3, Newspapers.com) — no Pennsylvania Quaker-specific curated links were returned |
| **No Quaker-specific indexed collection** | FamilySearch has no name-indexed Quaker meeting record collection for Pennsylvania in this period — Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia* and the manuscript repositories are the path in |

---

### Recommended Research Path

1. **Start with Hinshaw** — search *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* for published abstracts of the relevant monthly meeting
2. **Identify the meeting geographically** — determine which monthly meeting served the town/county where your ancestor lived (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, etc.)
3. **Browse the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes** on FamilySearch (Image Group 001188322) — browse-only, 145 images, 1750–1800
4. **Contact Swarthmore and Haverford** for manuscript monthly meeting registers not yet digitized
5. **Cross-check civil records** — search FamilySearch's Pennsylvania Probate Records (collection 1999196) and Compiled Marriages (collection 1502909) for corroborating evidence
6. **Check the 1790 census** for household enumeration and geographic confirmation

The combination of Hinshaw's abstracts, the Swarthmore and Haverford manuscript collections, and FamilySearch microfilm will cover the vast majority of what survives for Pennsylvania Quaker families in the late 1700s.
