# Locality Research Guide
## Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania — Late 1800s Steel Industry Era (c. 1870–1900)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Allegheny County** was formed in 1788 and contains Pittsburgh (the county seat). During the target period, the **City of Allegheny** — now Pittsburgh's North Side — was a legally separate municipality with its own records; it was not annexed into Pittsburgh until 1907. Steel mill towns ringing Pittsburgh (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Carnegie, Duquesne) were also incorporated separately, each generating their own local records. Always identify which municipality your ancestor lived in before assuming records are held together.

The county borders **Washington** (south), **Westmoreland** (east), **Butler** (north), **Beaver** (northwest), and **Lawrence** (northwest) counties. Workers living near these borders may have generated records on both sides — especially those in Homestead (near Westmoreland) or Ambridge/Freedom area (near Beaver/Butler).

---

### ⚠️ Critical Context: No Statewide Vital Registration in the Late 1800s

Pennsylvania had a brief, largely failed civil registration law (1852–1855) and **did not establish functioning statewide registration** until **1906**. For the 1870–1900 window, you should not expect to find official birth or death certificates. The FamilySearch collection **Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968** (collection 2255317) begins after the target period and will help only for deaths from 1906 onward. Church registers, census mortality schedules, and newspapers are your primary vital-record substitutes for this era.

> ⚠️ *Note: The Pennsylvania Vital Records and Pennsylvania Genealogy wiki pages returned only generic fallback content rather than Pennsylvania-specific guidance. The FamilySearch wiki page at* [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy) *is the recommended starting point for jurisdiction-specific guidance; the wiki_search tool returned verified excerpts from it.*

---

### 🏭 1. Industrial & Occupational Records *(Your Primary Focus)*

These are the records most distinctive to Pittsburgh's steel era. Coverage is fragmentary but irreplaceable.

| Source | What It Contains | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Company employment/payroll records** | Names, hire dates, wages, departments, sometimes birthplace | [Heinz History Center](https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org/) (Pittsburgh); [Rivers of Steel Archives](https://www.riversofsteel.com/) | Physical visit; some finding aids online |
| **Union membership records** | Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers (AAISW) membership, dues, lodge numbers | Heinz History Center; Pennsylvania State Archives | Physical visit |
| **City directories** | Name, occupation, employer, home address — issued annually | [Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh](https://www.carnegielibrary.org/) (holdings from 1810s); FamilySearch microfilm | Some digitized; many on Ancestry.com |
| **State factory inspector reports** | Annual reports listing factories, worker counts, accidents, sometimes names | Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg); Carnegie Library | Physical; some digitized by HathiTrust |
| **Federal census occupation columns** | Every household member's occupation listed in 1870, 1880, 1900 | FamilySearch; Ancestry.com; NARA | Fully indexed and online |

**Key repositories for industrial research:**
- **Senator John Heinz History Center**, 1212 Smallman St., Pittsburgh — the leading repository for western Pennsylvania industrial history, immigration records, and labor history.
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** — archives for U.S. Steel and predecessor companies; contact in advance.
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania Department** — runs of Pittsburgh Gazette, city directories, and local histories.

> *Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, "Industrial and Occupational Records" section — [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records)*

---

### 📋 2. Federal Census Records *(High Coverage — Fully Indexed Online)*

The federal census is your backbone for Pittsburgh families in this era and explicitly captures occupation.

| Census Year | Key Occupational/Industrial Fields | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **1870** | Occupation, real estate value, personal property | FamilySearch; Ancestry.com — fully indexed |
| **1880** | Occupation, relationship to head, birthplace of parents | FamilySearch (free); Ancestry.com — fully indexed |
| **1890** | ⚠️ Mostly destroyed by fire — severe gap | Fragments only at NARA |
| **1900** | Occupation, years in U.S., birthplace of parents, months employed | FamilySearch; Ancestry.com — fully indexed |

**Mortality schedules** (1870, 1880) record individuals who died in the year preceding the census, including cause of death — critical for mill accident victims.

---

### ✝️ 3. Church Records *(Essential Substitute for Vital Records)*

With no civil vital registration, church registers are often the **only** source for births, marriages, and burials in this period. Pittsburgh's steel workforce was overwhelmingly immigrant, and parishes were organized by ethnicity:

- **Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian**: Roman Catholic parishes — registers often held by individual parishes or diocesan archives (Diocese of Pittsburgh)
- **German workers**: German Lutheran (ELCA predecessors) and German Reformed churches
- **Irish workers**: Roman Catholic parishes

The **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** holds many sacramental registers. Individual parish registers may still be at the parish or have been transferred. The FamilySearch wiki_search result confirmed Catholic parishes are "often the best source for family data" for these immigrant communities.

> *Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy, "Immigration Records" section — [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)*

---

### 🛂 4. Naturalization & Immigration Records *(Partially Indexed Online)*

The steel mill wave drew massive immigration. FamilySearch has digitized a Pennsylvania-level volume of naturalization records:

| Volume | Record Type | Date Range | Images | Indexed | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 008120443 | Naturalization Records | 1790–1915 | 351 | **15% name-indexed** (English & German) | FamilySearch — partially searchable by name; remainder browse-only |

**Key locator note:** Pre-1906, any Pennsylvania court of record could grant naturalization. Allegheny County naturalizations are held at the **Allegheny County Courthouse** (Court of Common Pleas records) and the **National Archives at Philadelphia** (federal court naturalizations). The FamilySearch wiki confirmed naturalization records are at both repositories.

**Passenger lists** for immigrant steelworkers are at NARA (Ancestry.com and FamilySearch have these indexed).

---

### 💍 5. Marriage Records *(FamilySearch Collections — Indexed)*

FamilySearch holds three overlapping Pennsylvania marriage collections that cover the late 1800s:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950 (id: 1921317) | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | Indexed — searchable at FamilySearch |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (id: 1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | Indexed — searchable at FamilySearch |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (id: 1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | Indexed — searchable at FamilySearch |

Marriage licenses for Allegheny County are also held at the **Allegheny County Courthouse**.

---

### ⚖️ 6. Probate Records *(Browse-Only Images on FamilySearch)*

| Volume | Record Type | Date Range | Images | Indexed | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 008120441 | Probate Records | 1683–1994 | 1,180 | **0% — browse-only** | FamilySearch — must navigate image by image |

The FamilySearch collection **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (id: 1999196) is also available (893,214 records). Probate files can reveal an ancestor's occupation, property, and extended family. Original records are at the **Allegheny County Register of Wills**.

---

### ☠️ 7. Death Records *(Browse-Only + Post-Period Collection)*

| Volume | Record Type | Date Range | Images | Indexed | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 008120442 | Death Records | 1852–1968 | 674 | **0% — browse-only** | FamilySearch — must navigate image by image |

The statewide **Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968** collection begins after the target period (useful for deaths from 1906 onward but not for 1870–1905). For deaths in the 1870–1900 window, use: cemetery records (Find A Grave; [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)), newspaper obituaries, church burial registers, and the census mortality schedules.

---

### 📰 8. Newspapers

Pittsburgh's newspapers reported mill accidents, labor actions (including the famous 1892 Homestead Strike), and immigrant community news — and often published death notices:

- **Pittsburgh Gazette / Pittsburgh Post-Gazette** — digitized runs at Newspapers.com and GenealogyBank
- **Immigrant-language newspapers** (Polish, Slovak, Croatian) — check the Heinz History Center and Duquesne University's Gumberg Library

---

### 🏛️ Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | Holdings Relevant to Steel-Era Pittsburgh |
|---|---|
| **Senator John Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) | Company/employment records, union records, immigration files, city directories |
| **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area** (Pittsburgh) | U.S. Steel and predecessor company archives |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1810s+), newspapers, local history |
| **Allegheny County Courthouse** | Deed books, probate, marriage licenses, naturalizations |
| **Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Catholic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Factory inspector reports, state-level records |
| **National Archives at Philadelphia** | Federal naturalizations, passenger lists, federal court records |
| **FamilySearch** ([familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)) | Digitized volumes above; Pennsylvania marriage and probate collections |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census (1870–1900), city directories, passenger lists |

---

### ⚠️ Key Quirks & Gotchas

1. **No statewide birth/death registration exists for 1870–1900** — church registers and census mortality schedules are the primary substitutes.
2. **City of Allegheny was legally separate from Pittsburgh until 1907** — ancestors on Pittsburgh's North Side before annexation generated records under "City of Allegheny," not Pittsburgh.
3. **Mill towns were separate municipalities** — Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Carnegie each had their own local records; identify your ancestor's specific municipality before searching.
4. **Pre-1906 naturalizations could be in any court** — search both Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas AND federal court records at the National Archives at Philadelphia.
5. **FamilySearch naturalization volume (008120443) is only 15% name-indexed** and includes German-language records — browsing may be required for immigrant workers.
6. **Company employment records are fragmentary** — survival is uneven; contact the Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel before assuming records don't exist for a specific firm.
7. **Search adjoining counties for border-area mill towns** — Homestead is near Westmoreland County; Ambridge/Freedom-area workers may have records in Beaver County. Allegheny County's neighboring counties (Washington, Westmoreland, Butler, Beaver, Lawrence) were not confirmed in a tool result listing them; search each where geography warrants.
8. **The 1890 federal census is almost entirely destroyed** — a severe gap for this era; city directories and church records from 1889–1891 partially compensate.

---

Here is the locality research guide for Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania, focusing on the 1793 yellow fever epidemic:

---

# 📍 Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania
## Genealogy Research Guide — c. 1780–1810
### Focus: Families Affected by the 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic

**Jurisdiction:** Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania (standardPlace: *Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, United States*; established 1682)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Philadelphia County was established in 1682 and is coterminous with Philadelphia city. In August–November 1793, a yellow fever epidemic killed approximately **5,000 of Philadelphia's ~50,000 residents** — roughly one-tenth of the population — while thousands more fled the city. The epidemic was the deadliest in U.S. history and left a distinctive paper trail beyond the usual church registers: published death lists, hospital records, and relief committee minutes that name individual victims and their families. *(Wikipedia: "Yellow fever epidemic of 1793," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793)*

**Critical registration context:** Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration in 1793**. Statewide death registration did not begin until 1906 (evidenced by the Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection, 1906–1968). For 1793, **church records are the only contemporaneous vital records** for births, marriages, and burials.

---

## ⭐ Priority Sources for 1793 Epidemic Research

These sources are directly tied to the epidemic and are your first stops. They were identified via the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793):

### 1. Mathew Carey's Published Account
Physician and publisher Mathew Carey produced *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever...* (1793), which includes **printed lists of the dead by name** — the closest thing to a death register for the epidemic. Available digitized on HathiTrust and the Internet Archive; held in major genealogical libraries.

### 2. Citizens' Committee Minutes and Reports
The emergency Committee appointed by Philadelphia's citizens managed relief during the epidemic and kept **minutes and reports naming individuals who died, received aid, or fled**. Held at:
- **Philadelphia City Archives** (phila.gov/archives)
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** (hsp.org)

### 3. Bush Hill Hospital Records
Philadelphia's makeshift epidemic hospital produced **patient and mortality records** naming the sick and dead. Held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania**.

### 4. Church Burial Registers *(see full section below)*
Church burial registers are the primary vital records for 1793. Named in the wiki: **Christ Church** (Anglican/Episcopal) and **Gloria Dei / Old Swedes' Church** (Lutheran/Swedish) are among the best-documented for this period.

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 🏛️ Church Records *(Primary Source for 1793)*

Philadelphia's late 18th-century religious landscape was highly diverse, and each denomination maintained its own registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials. Key congregations include:

| Denomination | Congregation | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Anglican/Episcopal | Christ Church; St. Peter's | Burial registers survive; transcriptions published |
| Swedish Lutheran | Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') | Among oldest surviving registers in Philadelphia |
| Society of Friends (Quaker) | Multiple monthly meetings | Systematic birth/marriage/death records; well-organized |
| Presbyterian | First Presbyterian; Second Presbyterian | |
| German Lutheran | St. Michael's & Zion | German-language registers |
| German Reformed | Various | German-language registers |
| Catholic | St. Mary's; Old St. Joseph's | |
| Methodist | St. George's | |
| Jewish | Mikveh Israel | |

- The **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** (genpa.org) has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records and published transcriptions of colonial/early national registers. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records)*
- **Quaker (Friends) records** are especially systematic — monthly meeting minutes record births, marriages, and burials in organized volumes.
- Original registers are held by individual churches/denominational archives; microfilm copies are on FamilySearch. Researchers should search the **FamilySearch Catalog** directly for Philadelphia church microfilm, as the volume survey did not surface individual church registers.

**⚠️ Access note:** German-language registers (Lutheran, Reformed) require reading the original German.

---

### 📋 Vital Records (Civil Registration)

**No statewide civil registration existed in 1793.** Church records are the only contemporaneous source. The following civil collections on FamilySearch overlap the 1793 period but cover later eras for most records:

| Collection | FS ID | Date Range | Records | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 | 1999196 | 1683–1994 | 893,214 | 446,607 | **Indexed + images** |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 | 1571957 | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | 156,023 | **Indexed + images** |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 | 1502909 | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | 0 | **Index only — no images** |

- Pennsylvania Death Certificates (1906–1968) **post-date 1793** and are not applicable to the epidemic itself.
- Pennsylvania County Marriages (1885–1950) likewise **post-date 1793**.

---

### ⚖️ Probate Records *(High Priority for Epidemic Victims)*

A spike in 1793–1795 estate filings is expected given ~5,000 deaths. Probate is one of the strongest post-epidemic record classes.

- **FamilySearch collection — Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (id: **1999196**): 893,214 records, 446,607 images. Indexed and searchable at FamilySearch.org.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume** (imageGroupNumber: **008120441**): 1,180 images, probate records 1683–1994. **⚠️ Browse-only** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image; English language.
- Original records: **Philadelphia Register of Wills** (successor to the colonial Register of Wills).

---

### 🗳️ Census Records

| Census | Year | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1790 Federal Census | Pre-epidemic | Names heads of household; establishes who was in Philadelphia before the outbreak |
| 1800 Federal Census | Post-epidemic | Comparing to 1790 reveals households devastated by the epidemic — missing heads of household indicate death or permanent flight |

- **No mortality schedules for 1793** — mortality schedules accompany only the 1850–1885 federal censuses.
- Both censuses are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com.

---

### 📜 Land and Tax Records

- Philadelphia County deed books and tax records survive from the colonial era. **Tax lists are a substitute vital record** — a taxpayer who disappears after 1793 may have died in the epidemic or fled.
- Held at: **Philadelphia City Archives** and **Pennsylvania State Archives** (phmc.pa.gov).

---

### 🎖️ Military Records

- Many Philadelphia men served in the Revolutionary War (ended 1783). Pension files filed after 1793 can include family details — widows often filed for pensions after a husband died in the epidemic or shortly after.
- **Fold3** (fold3.com): Revolutionary War service records and pension files.
- **NARA** (archives.gov): Original pension files, RG 15 (Revolutionary War pensions).

---

### 📄 Naturalization Records

- **FamilySearch digitized volume** (imageGroupNumber: **008120443**): 351 images, Pennsylvania Naturalization Records, 1790–1915. **Partially searchable** — 15% name-indexed; remainder must be browsed. Not full-text searchable. English and German languages.
- Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any Pennsylvania court of record: Philadelphia District Court, Court of Common Pleas, etc.

---

### 📰 Newspapers *(High Value for 1793)*

Philadelphia newspapers published **death lists, estate sale notices, and family announcements** during and after the epidemic. Key titles active in 1793:
- *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*
- *The Pennsylvania Gazette*
- *General Advertiser*

**Access:**
- **Newspapers.com** — historical Philadelphia newspapers digitized and searchable
- **Readex / America's Historical Newspapers** — 18th-century papers
- **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** — original newspaper runs

---

### 🚢 Immigration and Passenger Records

Philadelphia was a major colonial-era port. German, Irish, and British immigration was ongoing through the 1790s.
- **NARA** (archives.gov) holds arrival records.
- Many are indexed on Ancestry.com and FamilySearch.
- Philadelphia immigrant arrivals are a useful corroborating source if an ancestor arrived shortly before or after 1793.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Philadelphia City Archives** (phila.gov/archives) | Committee minutes, early city records | In-person; some online |
| **Historical Society of Pennsylvania** (hsp.org) | Bush Hill records, Carey account, church records, manuscripts | In-person; some digital |
| **Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** (genpa.org) | Church record indexes and transcriptions | In-person; publications |
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (phmc.pa.gov) | Colonial/state records, tax lists, naturalization | In-person; some microfilm/digital |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Probate (indexed), marriages (indexed), naturalization, church microfilm | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal census, marriage compilations, immigration | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions for Philadelphia-area churchyards | Free online |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Revolutionary War pensions, military service records | Subscription |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal pension files, immigration, federal court records | In-person / some online |

---

## Neighboring Jurisdictions — Search These Too

Many residents fled the epidemic to surrounding areas; some died there or settled permanently. If an ancestor disappears from Philadelphia records in 1793, search:

- **Montgomery County, PA** (north/northwest)
- **Delaware County, PA** (southwest)
- **Bucks County, PA** (north)
- **Gloucester / Camden area, NJ** (across the Delaware River)

*Note: The Philadelphia County Genealogy FamilySearch Wiki page did not load during this survey — the Neighboring Counties table could not be confirmed from that source. The counties above reflect Philadelphia's known geographic borders.*

---

## Gaps and Coverage Warnings

- **FamilySearch Wiki pages** for Pennsylvania (all four sections: home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) and the Philadelphia County Genealogy page returned only generic content during this survey rather than Pennsylvania-specific guidance. Consult the wiki directly at:
  - https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy
  - https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Genealogy
- **The volume search** returned only 3 digitized volumes at the Pennsylvania state level — individual Philadelphia church registers on FamilySearch microfilm are not fully represented. Search the **FamilySearch Catalog** (https://www.familysearch.org/catalog) under "Philadelphia, Pennsylvania" for the full microfilm inventory.
- **No mortality schedules exist for 1793.**
- **No online curated external links** were returned specifically for Philadelphia by the FamilySearch external links tool — the six results were generic national resources.
- The **Probate Records digitized volume** (imageGroupNumber: 008120441) is **browse-only** — 1,180 images with no name index. Plan time for manual browsing if the indexed collection doesn't surface your ancestor.

---

## Suggested Research Sequence

1. **Mathew Carey's 1793 death list** — fastest confirmation of epidemic death
2. **Church burial registers** for the family's congregation (FamilySearch catalog + church/denominational archives)
3. **Probate records** filed 1793–1796 (FamilySearch collection 1999196, indexed)
4. **Compare 1790 and 1800 census** — household gaps reveal casualties or flight
5. **Philadelphia newspapers** for death notices and estate announcements
6. **Committee of Citizens minutes** at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania
7. **Search neighboring counties** (Montgomery, Delaware, Bucks, Gloucester/NJ) for refugees who did not return

---

# Locality Research Guide
## Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Fire Families, ca. 1855–1890

---

### Jurisdictional Context

**Cook County** was formed in 1831 from unorganized territory; Chicago was incorporated as a city in 1837. For the 1871 fire period, all local record-keeping — deeds, probate, court filings, birth and death registers — resided at the **Cook County Courthouse** in downtown Chicago.

> **⚠️ Critical research reality:** The Great Chicago Fire of October 8–10, 1871 destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and virtually all records housed there — deeds, probate files, birth and death registers, tax rolls, and court records. Approximately 300 people died and over 100,000 were left homeless. Researchers tracing Chicago families *before* October 1871 must expect near-total loss of locally created records and pivot immediately to substitute sources. Records created *after* the fire (from late October 1871 onward) are largely intact.

---

### Records That Survived — and What Was Lost

| Record Type | Pre-Fire Status | Post-Fire Status |
|---|---|---|
| Deeds / land records | **Destroyed** | Reconstructed under Burnt Record Act (1872) |
| Probate files | **Destroyed** | New filings from Nov 1871 onward intact |
| Birth & death registers | **Destroyed** | County registration resumed 1871 |
| Marriage licenses | **Destroyed** | County registration resumed 1871 |
| Court records (civil/criminal) | **Destroyed** | New docket from Nov 1871 onward |
| Tax rolls | **Destroyed** | Reconstructed from assessor notes |
| Federal censuses (1850, 1860, 1870) | **Survived** — originals held in Washington, D.C. | Not applicable |
| Many church registers | **Partially destroyed** — depended on parish location | Surviving/re-established parishes intact |
| City directories (1840s–1871) | **Largely survived** — copies held at Newberry Library | Continued annually |

---

### FamilySearch Collections (Indexed)

FamilySearch holds **4 indexed collections** for Cook County covering this period (scope: Illinois state-level, sourced from `collections_search`):

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Records | Dates |
|---|---|---|---|
| Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records | 1803978 | 285,000 | 1833–1925 |
| Illinois, Cook County, Birth Certificates | 2024189 | 1,450,000 | **1871**–1940 |
| Illinois, Cook County, Death Records | 1913456 | 980,000 | **1871**–1947 |
| Illinois, Cook County, Marriage Records | 1756321 | 620,000 | **1871**–1920 |

> **Note on vital records registration level:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Illinois Vital Records page returned generic content rather than the Illinois-specific article, so I cannot cite a specific state-registration start date from that source. What the collection data confirms is that **county-level** Cook County civil registration for births, deaths, and marriages begins at 1871 — the post-fire era. Illinois statewide registration did not begin until 1916; for the 1871 period, Cook County is where you look, not Springfield.

**Church records (1833–1925, 285K records)** are the most important collection for *pre-fire* events — parishes located outside the burn zone survived, and some re-registered sacramental records from memory or secondary copies after the fire.

---

### Digitized Volumes on FamilySearch

`volume_search` returned **2 digitized volumes** for Cook County, 1855–1890 (2 total results):

| Volume | Image Group | Images | Indexed? | Record Type | Dates |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-fire court records (reconstructed) | 009982110 | 38 | **0% — browse-only** | Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies) | 1865–1871 |
| Post-fire property re-recordings | 009982111 | 112 | **41% indexed** | Post-fire Property Re-recordings | 1871–1880 |

- **Volume 009982110** must be browsed image-by-image — there is no name search. These are reconstructed copies of pre-fire court records, not originals.
- **Volume 009982111** is 41% name-indexed on FamilySearch; the remaining 59% requires browsing. This is the digitized version of the **Burnt Record Act** re-recordings.

---

### Substitute Sources for Pre-Fire Research

These are the primary routes around the record loss, confirmed by the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire):

#### 1. Federal Census Records — ⭐ Highest priority
The **1850, 1860, and 1870 federal census schedules for Chicago survived intact** because the originals were held in Washington, D.C. The 1870 census is especially valuable as a snapshot of the family just one year before the fire.
- Also check **mortality schedules** (1850–1880) for deaths in the year preceding each census.
- Available indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.com.

#### 2. Burnt Record Act Reconstructions (1872) — Property
The Illinois legislature passed the **Burnt Record Act of 1872** requiring property owners to re-register deeds. These reconstructed filings are the primary substitute for pre-fire land and property records.
- Digitized in FamilySearch volume **009982111** (112 images, 41% indexed).
- Physical originals and fuller holdings at the **Chicago History Museum** (see Repositories).

#### 3. Chicago Title and Trust Company Records
Insurance company records — particularly those of the **Chicago Title and Trust Company** — documented property ownership extensively around the fire period. The collection is held at the **Chicago History Museum** and is a major substitute for destroyed deed records.

#### 4. Church Records — Surviving Parishes
Many Catholic and Protestant parishes located outside the burn zone retained their registers. The **Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** holds Catholic parish registers; FamilySearch collection **1803978** (Church Records, 1833–1925, 285K records) provides indexed access to many of these.

#### 5. City Directories (1840s–1871)
Annual Chicago city directories survived the fire and are held at the **Newberry Library**. They name heads of household with addresses and occupations — invaluable for confirming residence and tracking mobility before and after the fire.

#### 6. Newspapers
Historical Chicago newspapers (the *Chicago Tribune*, *Chicago Times*, and others) reported extensively on fire victims, relief efforts, and displaced families. Published lists of the dead and homeless appeared in the days after the fire.
- **Newspapers.com** and **Chronicling America** (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) carry digitized Illinois newspapers.
- The Newberry Library holds extensive Chicago newspaper holdings.

#### 7. Military Records (Civil War veterans)
Many 1871 Chicagoans were Civil War veterans. **Pension files at NARA** and service records on **Fold3.com** (fold3.com) are unaffected by the fire and provide biographical detail, family information, and post-war addresses.

#### 8. Federal Land Records (Pre-urban)
For families who arrived before Chicago's rapid urbanization, **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office** records (glorecords.blm.gov) document original federal land patents — unaffected by the courthouse fire.

---

### Post-Fire Records (Late 1871 Onward) — Intact

Once you move past the fire date, Cook County records resume normally:

| Record Type | Where to Search | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Birth certificates (1871–) | FamilySearch collection 2024189 (1.45M records) | County-level registration |
| Death records (1871–) | FamilySearch collection 1913456 (980K records) | County-level registration |
| Marriage records (1871–) | FamilySearch collection 1756321 (620K records) | County-level registration |
| Probate records (post-fire) | IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University | New filings from late 1871 |
| Court/naturalization records | IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University | Pre-1906 naturalizations in any court of record |
| Cemetery records | FindAGrave (findagrave.com) | Many Chicago cemeteries documented |

---

### Key Repositories

Sourced from the FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Repositories):

| Repository | Holdings Relevant to 1871 Research |
|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** (Chicago) | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, newspapers — largely survived the fire |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title and Trust insurance records, Burnt Record Act papers, photographs, personal papers of fire survivors |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County records post-1871: probate, court, naturalization |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (pre- and post-fire; surviving parishes); also available via FamilySearch collection 1803978 |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871 onward (originals) |
| **National Archives, Great Lakes Region (Chicago)** | Federal census, naturalization, military records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Microfilmed and digitized post-fire Cook County records; church records; federal census |

---

### Neighboring Counties

Families displaced by the fire often relocated to suburban Cook County townships or neighboring counties. Check records in:

- **DuPage County, Illinois** (west)
- **Lake County, Illinois** (north)
- **Will County, Illinois** (south)
- **Kane County, Illinois** (west)

> The Cook County Genealogy page's *Neighboring Counties* table was not returned by the wiki_read call (which resolved to a generic page), so the above neighbors reflect the county's geographic position. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy for the full table.

---

### Research Strategy Summary

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census** — the last pre-fire snapshot. Note exact address, neighbors, and household composition.
2. **Search the 1860 and 1850 censuses** backward to establish the family before Chicago.
3. **Check FamilySearch church records collection (1803978)** for any pre-fire baptisms, marriages, or burials — surviving parish registers are your best pre-1871 vital record substitute.
4. **Search Chicago city directories** at the Newberry Library for residence and occupation, year by year up to 1871 and after.
5. **For property owners:** Search the Burnt Record Act re-recordings (FamilySearch volume 009982111, 41% indexed) and the Chicago History Museum's Title and Trust holdings.
6. **Check newspapers.com/Chronicling America** for fire-era reporting — victim lists, relief rosters, notices of missing persons.
7. **After the fire:** Resume with Cook County birth (2024189), death (1913456), and marriage (1756321) collections on FamilySearch — all start from 1871.
8. **Civil War veterans:** Pull pension files and service records on Fold3 regardless of the fire — these are untouched federal records.

> **Key quirk:** Do not assume any Cook County *locally created* record from before October 1871 survives — the working assumption must be destruction unless a specific surviving source (church register, city directory, federal record) is confirmed. The 1870 federal census is always your pre-fire anchor.

---

## Locality Research Guide: Louisiana, French Colonial Period (1699–1762)

### Jurisdictional Context

French Louisiana (*La Louisiane*) was an administrative district of **New France**, under French authority from 1682. New Orleans was founded in 1718 and served as the colonial capital and the center of record-keeping throughout the period. In 1762, by the Treaty of Fontainebleau, France secretly ceded Louisiana west of the Mississippi to Spain; the eastern portion went to Britain. Spanish administration ran 1762–1800, France briefly reclaimed the territory 1800–1803, and the Louisiana Purchase transferred it to the United States in 1803.

**Two critical facts that shape every record type for this period:**
1. **No civil registration existed.** Births, marriages, and burials were recorded exclusively by the Catholic Church, the only legally recognized church in French Louisiana.
2. **The Code Noir** (Black Code) required the Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, making church registers a source for enslaved individuals as well as free settlers.

Records generated during the French period were administered by the **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)** and the Catholic parishes. There were no parishes-as-counties yet — that administrative structure came later under American governance.

---

### Record Types, Availability, and Access

#### 1. 🏛️ Catholic Parish Registers (Baptisms, Marriages, Burials)
**The primary source for vital events throughout the entire colonial period.**

- The **St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans** holds registers from **1720**, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy – French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) — returned by `collections_search` with 987,654 records and 493,827 images. Date range starts in 1718, fully within the French colonial window.
- ⚠️ Records are written in **French** (and some Latin for sacramental entries). Researchers must read the original language or use a translator.
- 🔍 **Access:** FamilySearch (searchable online); the originals are at St. Louis Cathedral Archives, New Orleans.

#### 2. ⚖️ Superior Council Records
**The colonial government's administrative and judicial records — a rich substitute for missing vital and property records.**

- Contains: **land grants (concessions)**, court proceedings, contracts, and **estate inventories**.
- Held at the **Louisiana Historical Center**, Old U.S. Mint building, New Orleans — partially digitized, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy – French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- ⚠️ Digitization is partial; physical access or microfilm may be needed for the full run.
- 🔍 **Access:** Louisiana Historical Center (in person or inquire about digital surrogates).

#### 3. 📜 Notarial Records
**The oldest continuously operating notarial office in North America — one of the most important colonial sources.**

- The **New Orleans Notarial Archives** holds contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions **from the 1730s** onward, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property – Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)).
- The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** provides public access.
- FamilySearch has **1 digitized volume** of Orleans Parish notarial acts (imageGroupNumber `004990115`): 167 images, covering 1803–1820 — just after the French colonial period ends, but establishing the continuous series. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — browse-only, image by image. Languages: French and English.
- ⚠️ For the core 1699–1762 window, no FamilySearch-indexed notarial volumes were returned; the physical archives are the primary access point.

#### 4. 🌾 Land Records / Colonial Concessions
**Essential for placing families on the landscape and tracing property descent.**

- French land concessions and later Spanish land grants are documented in the **American State Papers: Public Lands** series.
- The **Louisiana State Land Office** holds additional records.
- Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Land and Property – Colonial Land Grants](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)): French concessions follow French legal traditions, not English common law — titles descend differently and researchers should account for this when tracing inheritance.
- 🔍 **Access:** American State Papers are digitized (HathiTrust, Library of Congress); Louisiana State Land Office for state-held records.

#### 5. 🗒️ Probate Records
**Wills and estate inventories can document family structure when vital records are missing.**

- **FamilySearch collection:** *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* (collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)) — returned by `collections_search` with 456,789 records and 228,394 images. Date range begins **1756**, within the French colonial period.
- These records were administered under French legal tradition (civil law, not common law), so the documents may read differently from English-style probate files.

#### 6. 🇫🇷 French National Archives (ANOM) — Overseas Records
**For administrative, military, and census-type records, the key repository is in France.**

- The **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France, holds **administrative correspondence and census rolls** for colonial Louisiana, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Louisiana Genealogy – French Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records)).
- Colonial censuses (*recensements*) and passenger/settler lists may appear here that are not available in U.S. repositories.
- 🔍 **Access:** ANOM online catalog at [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr); some series digitized.

#### 7. 🪖 Military and Emigration Records
- French colonial soldiers and settlers were documented in French military and emigration records, also likely at ANOM and the Archives Nationales in Paris (Série C13 covers Louisiana).
- Passenger lists for settlers arriving in Louisiana exist for some periods; the Sauvole and Bienville-era settlement records are partially published in genealogical literature.
- **Fold3.com** (returned by `external_links_search`) holds some U.S.-era military records but coverage does not reach the French colonial period.

---

### Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Church Records 1718–1925; Probate Records 1756–1984; 1 notarial volume (1803–1820) | Free online |
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (New Orleans) | Superior Council records; partially digitized | In person / inquire |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial acts from 1730s | In person; some online |
| **St. Louis Cathedral Archives** (New Orleans) | Parish registers from 1720 | In person / via FamilySearch |
| **ANOM** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Colonial admin, census rolls, correspondence | Online catalog; partial digitization |
| **Archives Nationales** (Paris) — Série C13 | Louisiana colonial administration | In-person / online catalog |
| **Louisiana State Land Office** | Land concessions, later grants | State agency |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Post-1803 federal records; some territorial materials | Online and in person |

---

### Key Research Quirks

- **Language barrier:** Virtually all French colonial records are in French (sacramental entries may be in Latin). Proficiency in colonial French — including archaic abbreviations and script — is needed to read originals.
- **No civil registration for this period.** The Catholic Church is your only source of baptism, marriage, and burial data for 1699–1762. Do not expect a civil birth or death certificate.
- **Jurisdiction shift mid-century:** In 1762, Louisiana transferred to Spanish authority. If your ancestor's activity straddles 1762, record types and language may shift (Spanish colonial records, including *padrones*/census rolls, appear from the 1760s). Search both the French-era and Spanish-era series as a continuous trail.
- **Parish vs. county:** During the French period, administrative units were not the modern Louisiana parishes (counties). Records are organized around the colonial capital (New Orleans) and Catholic parishes — not by county-level geography.
- **Code Noir and enslaved persons:** Catholic baptismal registers are often the only documentary evidence for enslaved individuals in this period. Seek them in the same church registers as free persons.
- **FamilySearch digitization gap:** The volume_search returned only 1 volume for this region and period — the core 1699–1762 French colonial window is largely **not digitized or indexed** on FamilySearch. Physical archives (Louisiana Historical Center, Notarial Archives, ANOM) are essential.
- **FamilySearch Wiki Louisiana-specific pages** (Vital Records, Church Records, Land and Property, Notarial Records, Probate Records) returned only generic fallback content in this survey — consult them directly at [familysearch.org/wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/wiki) for any updates to digitization status.

---

### Where to Start

1. **Church registers first** — search the *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* collection on FamilySearch ([collection 1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) for any baptism, marriage, or burial entries.
2. **Notarial Archives** — if your family was in New Orleans or nearby, contracts and estate documents at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center can fill major gaps.
3. **Superior Council records** at the Louisiana Historical Center for land, court, and estate matters.
4. **ANOM (France)** for administrative and census materials not held in Louisiana — especially useful for immigrant origins and settler rosters.
5. **Published genealogical literature** — Louisiana French colonial genealogy has a strong body of compiled work (e.g., *Acadian Genealogy* sources, the work of Winston De Ville) that can shortcut searches in original records.

---

# Locality Research Guide: Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns, Late 1800s (c. 1870–1900)

## Jurisdictional Overview

Pennsylvania's coal mining heartland spans two distinct regions:

**Anthracite (Hard Coal) — Northeastern PA** — the primary focus for most researchers:
| County | Formed | Key Towns | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill | 1811 | Pottsville, Mahanoy City, Shenandoah, Minersville | Core anthracite county |
| Luzerne | 1786 | Wilkes-Barre, Hazleton, Pittston, Nanticoke | Large county; parent of Lackawanna |
| **Lackawanna** | **1878** | **Scranton, Carbondale** | **Carved from Luzerne — records before 1878 are in Luzerne** |
| Carbon | 1843 | Mauch Chunk (Jim Thorpe), Lansford, Tamaqua | Formed from Northampton & Monroe |
| Northumberland | 1772 | Shamokin, Mount Carmel | Significant coal operations |

**Bituminous (Soft Coal) — Western PA:** Westmoreland, Fayette, Washington, and Allegheny counties. Record types are similar but historical societies differ.

**Population context:** The region drew massive immigrant waves — Irish and Welsh (1820s–1860s), then Germans; followed by Poles, Lithuanians, Slovaks, Italians, and Ukrainians in the 1880s–1900s. This heavily influences which church records and foreign-language sources exist. *(Source: Wikipedia, [Coal Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region))*

---

## ⚠️ Critical Quirk: No Statewide Vital Registration Until 1906

Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births or deaths until **1906**. For the entire late-1800s research window, this means:

- **Birth and death records before 1906 are primarily found in church registers**, not civil government records.
- Philadelphia had county-level registration from 1860; Allegheny County from 1870. The anthracite coal counties had **no civil birth/death registration** in this period.
- **Marriage records** are the exception — kept at the county level from the colonial period (licenses/bonds at the county courthouse). *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records))*

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. 🏭 Mining Company & Occupational Records — *The Unique Source Class*

These records are the defining feature of coal region research and have no equivalent elsewhere.

| Record Type | Coverage | Access | Digitization |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Mine Inspector Annual Reports** | Statewide from 1870; fatal accidents list name, age, nationality, cause of death | Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg); FamilySearch Wiki: [Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining) | Physical / microfilm |
| **Mine Worker Employment Cards** (Schuylkill Co.) | 1870–1900, 410 images | FamilySearch vol. 002240015 | ✅ **Indexed + images** (95% name-indexed, full-text searchable) |
| **Mine Accident Reports** (Luzerne Co.) | 1870–1895, 287 images | FamilySearch vol. 002240016 | 🔍 **Browse-only** (0% indexed, no full-text) |
| **Colliery Payroll Ledgers** (Lackawanna Co.) | 1878–1900, 199 images | FamilySearch vol. 002240017 | 🔍 **Browse-only** (0% indexed, no full-text) |
| **Company employment records / pay ledgers** (fragmentary) | Varies by colliery | Pennsylvania State Archives; Historical Society of Schuylkill County; Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) | Physical only |
| **UMWA Union records** | 1890+ (union founded 1890) | Membership rolls and grievance files; Anthracite Heritage Museum | Physical only |

> **Note:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 23 total digitized volumes for Pennsylvania 1870–1900; only 3 are detailed above (first page). A researcher should request additional pages or browse FamilySearch directly for the full set.

---

### 2. ⛪ Church Records — *The Essential Substitute for Civil Registration*

Because there was no civil birth/death registration before 1906, **ethnic parish registers are the primary source** for vital events. The coal region had dense networks of ethnically organized congregations.

| Ethnic Community | Denominations | Key Repositories |
|---|---|---|
| Irish | Roman Catholic | Diocese of Allentown (Schuylkill/Carbon/Lehigh); Diocese of Scranton (Luzerne/Lackawanna) |
| Welsh | Congregational, Welsh Calvinist Methodist, Baptist | Historical Society of Pennsylvania; local church archives |
| German | Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic | Lutheran Theological Seminary Archives; local parishes |
| Polish | Roman Catholic | Diocese of Scranton; individual parish archives |
| Lithuanian | Roman Catholic | Diocese of Scranton |
| Slovak | Roman Catholic, Greek Catholic | Individual parish archives |
| Italian | Roman Catholic | Diocesan archives |
| Ukrainian / Rusyn | Greek Catholic, Orthodox | Byzantine Catholic Archeparchy of Pittsburgh; Orthodox Church in America records |

**FamilySearch collections covering church records within the target period:**
- *Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950* — [collection 1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) — 524,189 records; overlaps target window
- *Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950* — [collection 1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) — 312,045 records
- *Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900* — [collection 1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) — 198,765 records (abstracts; no images)

> **Language warning:** Ukrainian, Slovak, Polish, and Lithuanian parish registers from this period are often in Latin or the vernacular language — not English. Plan for translation.

---

### 3. 📊 Census Records

| Record | Years | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Federal Census** | 1870, 1880, 1900 (1890 destroyed) | Lists occupation as "miner" — key for identifying coal families. FamilySearch and Ancestry both indexed. |
| **Mortality Schedules** | 1870, 1880 | List deaths in the prior year; name, age, occupation, cause — especially useful for mine accident victims |
| **Pennsylvania State Census** | None for this period | Pennsylvania did not conduct state censuses in the late 1800s |

---

### 4. 🛂 Immigration & Naturalization Records — *Critical for This Population*

Given the massive immigrant influx, these are among the most valuable record classes.

- **Passenger arrival lists:** Primarily through Philadelphia (pre-1870s) and New York (Castle Garden 1855–1890, Ellis Island from 1892). Available indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry; NARA holds the originals. *(Source: NARA, [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/))*
- **Naturalization records (pre-1906):** Filed in **any court of record** — county courts of common pleas, federal district courts, orphans' courts. Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**. Search the specific county courthouse as well. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources))*
- **After 1906:** Naturalizations were centralized through the federal Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization — NARA holds these.

---

### 5. 📜 Vital Records (County-Level Marriage Records)

As noted above, only **marriage** records were consistently created at the county level during this period.

- **Marriage licenses and bonds:** County courthouse, Register of Deeds/Recorder of Deeds
- **FamilySearch:** See marriage collections listed under Church Records above
- **Birth and death records:** Not available through civil registration for this period; use church records or cemetery records as primary sources

---

### 6. ⚖️ Probate Records

- *Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994* — [collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — 893,214 records; held at county Register of Wills
- Useful for: identifying heirs, family relationships, property (company housing/lots were common in mining towns), and real estate holdings

---

### 7. 🗺️ Land & Property Records

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Pennsylvania Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Land_Records))*
- County **deed books** at the county Recorder of Deeds — track company-owned patches and individual lot purchases
- **Pennsylvania State Land Office** (Harrisburg) holds warrant, survey, and patent records back to the colonial period
- **Tax assessment records** survive from the colonial era in many counties and serve as census substitutes; held at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives

---

### 8. 🏛️ Court Records (Naturalizations, Guardianships, Name Changes)

- County Courts of Common Pleas: naturalization declarations and petitions, guardianships of minor orphans after mine accidents, name change petitions (very common among Eastern European immigrants anglicizing names)
- Physical records at county courthouses; some microfilmed at the Pennsylvania State Archives

---

### 9. 🎖️ Military Records

- Civil War pension files at NARA are a rich source for miners who served; pensions continued through the 1900s
- NARA, [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) — service records, pension files
- Fold3, [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/) — digitized military records

---

### 10. 📰 Newspapers

- The coal region had robust local newspaper coverage; **mine disasters, accidents, and labor strikes** were extensively reported
- Names, ages, and nationalities of accident victims frequently appear
- Newspapers.com, [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) — digitized historical newspapers
- Pennsylvania State Library and local historical societies hold physical runs

---

### 11. ⚰️ Cemetery Records

- Find A Grave, [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) — crowdsourced cemetery records; coal region cemeteries are well represented
- Ethnic fraternal societies (e.g., Polish National Alliance, Lithuanian Alliance) often maintained their own cemetery sections

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings Relevant to Coal Region Research |
|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg) | Mine Inspector reports (1870+), naturalization records, land office records, tax records, state government records |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville) | Local mining records, newspapers, family files, company records |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton / Lackawanna Co.) | Mining company records, UMWA records, immigrant community collections |
| **Diocese of Scranton Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland counties |
| **Diocese of Allentown Archives** | Catholic parish registers for Schuylkill, Carbon, Lehigh counties |
| **County Courthouses** (Pottsville, Wilkes-Barre, Scranton, Mauch Chunk) | Deeds, wills, marriage licenses, naturalization records |
| **NARA Philadelphia** | Federal court naturalizations post-1906, some census records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indexed collections and digitized volumes listed above |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census, [U.S. Federal Census Collection](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) |

---

## Digitization Status Summary

| Record Class | Digitization Level |
|---|---|
| Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill) | ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch) |
| Federal Census 1870, 1880, 1900 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Pennsylvania County Marriages (to 1900) | ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch) |
| Pennsylvania Probate Records | ✅ Indexed + images (FamilySearch) |
| Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne) | 🔍 Browse-only images (FamilySearch) |
| Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna) | 🔍 Browse-only images (FamilySearch) |
| Church registers (ethnic parishes) | ⚠️ Varies widely; many physical-only at diocesan archives |
| Mine Inspector Annual Reports (1870+) | 📁 Physical / microfilm at PA State Archives |
| Naturalization records (pre-1906) | 📁 Physical at county courthouses / PA State Archives |
| UMWA union records | 📁 Physical at Anthracite Heritage Museum |
| Pennsylvania Birth/Death Certificates | ❌ Civil registration does not begin until 1906 — use church records |

---

## Key Research Gotchas

1. **Lackawanna County records before 1878 are in Luzerne County.** If your ancestor lived in Scranton or Carbondale before 1878, search Luzerne County first.
2. **No statewide birth or death registration before 1906.** Ethnic church registers are your primary source for vital events in the late 1800s.
3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations can appear in any court of record.** Check county courts, not just federal courts.
4. **Name anglicization is very common.** Eastern European immigrants often used anglicized or phonetically spelled names in English-language records vs. their native-language parish registers — search both.
5. **FamilySearch volume_search returned 23 digitized volumes** for Pennsylvania 1870–1900; only 3 are detailed above (first page of results). Browse FamilySearch directly for the full set of mining region volumes.
6. **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for specific PA counties** (Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon) returned only generic content in this session — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at familysearch.org/wiki for county-specific guidance, as the pages may contain more detail than was returned here.

---

No active research project was detected, so this guide is presented as a standalone reference. If you'd like to start a project, narrow to a specific county or ancestor, or move into planning actual searches, just say the word!

# 📜 Locality Research Guide
## Massachusetts — Early Puritan Settlements (c. 1620–1700)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

The early 1600s in Massachusetts involved **two distinct colonial jurisdictions**, which matters deeply for where records were created and are now held:

| Colony | Founded | Ended | Notes |
|--------|---------|-------|-------|
| **Plymouth Colony** | 1620 | 1691 | Founded by Pilgrims; had its own courts and records system |
| **Massachusetts Bay Colony** | 1628 | 1691 | Puritan settlers under Governor John Winthrop; ~20,000 arrivals in the Great Migration of 1630–1640 |
| **Province of Massachusetts Bay** | 1691 | — | Created when Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay merged |

The first four **counties** in Massachusetts Bay were established in **1643**: Suffolk, Middlesex, Essex, and Norfolk/Barnstable. Records before that date were kept at the colony level. Plymouth Colony maintained its own separate court structure throughout its existence.

> ⚠️ Know which colony your ancestor lived in — they had separate record systems. Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational]

---

### Record Types Available

#### 1. 🏛️ Town Vital Records — **Digitized & Indexed**

| | |
|--|--|
| **FamilySearch Collection** | *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* — Collection ID [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) |
| **Date range** | 1620–1890 |
| **Registration level** | **Town level**, mandated from **1639** |

Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated that towns record births, marriages, and deaths from **1639** — one of the earliest civil registration systems in North America. Records were kept by the **town clerk** through town meeting minutes. [Sources: Wikipedia, *Massachusetts Bay Colony*; FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy, Colonial Vital Records: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records]

A critical finding aid for this period is the **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850"** series (the Tanner–Corbin series) — published abstracts covering **over 200 Massachusetts towns**, drawing from original town clerk records. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records]

**Where held:** Original records at the Massachusetts Archives (Boston) and local town clerks; published abstracts widely available in libraries and on FamilySearch.

> ⚠️ Registration was at the **town level** — always search by town, not by county.

---

#### 2. ⛪ Church Records — **Digitized & Indexed**

| | |
|--|--|
| **FamilySearch Collection** | *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* — Collection ID [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) |
| **Date range** | 1630–1920 |

Congregational (Puritan) churches were the **established church** of the colony. As such, church records are essential — often the richest source for the 1620–1700 period. Registers contain:
- Membership lists
- Baptisms
- Marriages
- Disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments)

Many early church records have been published in the **Colonial Society of Massachusetts** series and local historical society publications. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records, Congregational: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational]

**Where held:** Denominational archives, local historical societies, Massachusetts Archives, NEHGS.

---

#### 3. 📜 Probate Records — **Digitized & Indexed**

| | |
|--|--|
| **FamilySearch Collection** | *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* — Collection ID [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) |
| **Date range** | 1635–1991 |

County probate courts begin in the **1630s**. Records include wills, estate inventories, guardianship appointments, and letters of administration — invaluable for reconstructing family relationships and wealth in the colonial period. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki search results]

**Where held:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives; FamilySearch online collection.

---

#### 4. 🗺️ Land Records (Deeds)

County deed registries survive in **remarkably complete runs from the 1630s**, recorded at the county level. This is one of the strongest record series for early Massachusetts families. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Church Records search result]

**Counties and their formation dates:**
- Suffolk (1643) — Boston area
- Middlesex (1643)
- Essex (1643)
- Norfolk / Barnstable (1643)

**Where held:** County Registries of Deeds; Massachusetts Archives.

> ⚠️ **Digitization gap:** The volume search did not surface any digitized land deed volumes for the 1620–1700 period. Verify current FamilySearch holdings directly and plan for on-site or microfilm access at county registries or the Massachusetts Archives.

---

#### 5. 🏛️ Court and Colony Records

The **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) holds original colony records from the **1620s onward**, including:
- Governor's correspondence
- Court of Assistants records (criminal jurisdiction)
- County court records (civil and minor criminal)
- General Court (legislative) records

These are foundational for any serious colonial Massachusetts research. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records]

---

#### 6. 🚢 Immigration / Passenger Lists

Pre-1820 federal passenger lists do not exist. For the colonial period, the key resources are:

- **"The Great Migration" study series** (NEHGS): Documents every known settler who arrived **1620–1643**, with detailed biographical and family sketches. This should be the **first stop** for anyone with a Great Migration ancestor. [Source: FamilySearch Wiki — Massachusetts Genealogy]
- **James Savage, *Genealogical Dictionary of the First Settlers of New England*** (4 vols.): A classic compiled finding aid.
- **John Camden Hotten, *Original Lists of Persons of Quality***: Covers some 17th-century migrants.

> ⚠️ FamilySearch Collection *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* (ID: 1784312) does **not** cover this period — dates begin 1820.

---

#### 7. 🪖 Military Records

Colonial-era military records are limited. Consult:
- Massachusetts Archives (muster rolls, colonial militia records)
- Published transcriptions of **King Philip's War (1675–1676)** muster rolls
- National Archives (NARA) for later periods

---

#### 8. 📰 Newspapers

Newspapers **do not apply** to the 1620–1700 period. Massachusetts's first newspaper (*Boston News-Letter*) was not established until **1704**.

---

#### 9. Census Records

**No federal census applies** — enumeration began in 1790. Substitutes for population-level research in this period:
- Town meeting records
- Tax and valuation lists
- Church membership rolls
- Probate and land records

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds for This Period |
|-----------|-------------------------------|
| **Massachusetts Archives**, Boston | Colony records, court records, governor's correspondence from 1620s onward |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)**, Boston | Great Migration series, manuscript collections, published genealogies — the largest genealogical library in New England |
| **American Antiquarian Society**, Worcester | Published colonial records and historical materials |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Land deed books from 1630s |
| **Pilgrim Hall Museum**, Plymouth | Plymouth Colony materials |
| **FamilySearch** (online) | Town Vital Records 1620–1890, Church Records 1630–1920, Probate Records 1635–1991 |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (post-1790 only); some colonial-era compiled databases |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery records |
| **NARA** | Federal records (post-1776 primarily) |

---

### Online Access Summary

| Record Type | Online Access | Notes |
|------------|--------------|-------|
| Town Vital Records | ✅ Indexed — FamilySearch #2061550 | Search by town |
| Church Records | ✅ Indexed — FamilySearch #1921657 | Congregational registers |
| Probate Records | ✅ Indexed — FamilySearch #1678901 | From 1635 |
| Land / Deed Records | ⚠️ Digitization extent not confirmed | County registries; MA Archives |
| Court / Colony Records | ⚠️ Not confirmed online | Massachusetts Archives |
| Passenger Lists (colonial) | ❌ No pre-1820 lists | Use NEHGS Great Migration series |
| Plymouth Colony records | Published / indexed separately | Not integrated with MA Bay records |
| Census | ❌ Not applicable pre-1790 | Use tax lists, church rolls |

---

### Research Quirks to Know

1. **Two colonies, two record systems** — Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony operated separately until 1691. Identify your ancestor's colony first.
2. **Town-level registration from 1639** — vital records are filed at the **town**, not the county. Always search by town.
3. **Plymouth Colony records published separately** — do not expect them to be integrated with Massachusetts Bay Colony records.
4. **"Great Migration" series is the essential starting point** for any 1620–1643 ancestor — NEHGS documented every known settler.
5. **County land and probate records begin 1643** — before that date, records were kept at the colony level.
6. **No census before 1790** — use tax/valuation lists, church rolls, and town meeting records as substitutes.
7. **FamilySearch Wiki** — the Massachusetts-specific wiki pages (Vital Records, Church Records, Land, Probate) returned generic fallback content during this survey. Consult [Massachusetts Genealogy on FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy) directly for the most current guidance.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Massachusetts Early Puritan Settlements (c. 1620–1700)
## Locality Research Guide

### Jurisdictional Context

The early 1600s in Massachusetts involved two distinct colonial jurisdictions:

- **Plymouth Colony** (1620–1691): Founded by the Pilgrims at Plymouth. Had its own courts, laws, and records system.
- **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (1628–1691): Founded by Puritan settlers; governed from Boston. Required towns to record vital events from 1639. ~20,000 settlers arrived in the Great Migration of 1630–1640.
- **Province of Massachusetts Bay** (1691–): Formed when Plymouth Colony and Massachusetts Bay Colony merged.

The first four counties in Massachusetts Bay were established in 1643: Suffolk, Middlesex, Essex, and Norfolk/Barnstable. Records before that date were kept at the colony level. Plymouth Colony maintained its own court structure throughout its existence.

### 1. Town Vital Records — Digitized & Indexed

FamilySearch: *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (Collection ID 2061550). Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated town-level recording of births, marriages, and deaths from 1639 — one of the earliest civil registration systems in North America. The "Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series (Tanner–Corbin) provides published abstracts for 200+ towns. Search by town, not county. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records]

### 2. Church Records — Digitized & Indexed

FamilySearch: *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (Collection ID 1921657). Congregational (Puritan) churches were the established church of the colony. Registers contain membership lists, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary proceedings. Many published in the Colonial Society of Massachusetts series. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational]

### 3. Probate Records — Digitized & Indexed

FamilySearch: *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* (Collection ID 1678901). County probate courts begin in the 1630s with wills, inventories, guardianship, and administration records.

### 4. Land Records (Deeds)

County deed registries survive in complete runs from the 1630s. Recorded at the county level (counties formed 1643). Held at County Registries of Deeds and Massachusetts Archives. Digitization extent for 1620–1700 not confirmed by volume_search.

### 5. Court and Colony Records

Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds colony records from the 1620s: governor's correspondence, Court of Assistants, county courts, General Court records. [Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records]

### 6. Plymouth Colony Records

Separate from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. Published in Nathaniel Shurtleff's *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (12 vols). After 1691, absorbed into Plymouth County, MA.

### 7. Immigration / Compiled Sources

No pre-1820 federal passenger lists. Use: NEHGS "Great Migration" series (every known settler 1620–1643); James Savage, *Genealogical Dictionary of the First Settlers of New England* (4 vols); John Camden Hotten, *Original Lists of Persons of Quality*. FamilySearch Passenger Lists collection (ID 1784312) begins 1820 — does not cover this period.

### 8. No Census Before 1790

Substitute with tax/valuation lists, church membership rolls, and town meeting records.

### Key Repositories

- Massachusetts Archives, Boston: Colony records from 1620s
- NEHGS, Boston: Great Migration series, largest genealogical library in New England
- American Antiquarian Society, Worcester
- County Registries of Deeds
- Pilgrim Hall Museum, Plymouth
- FamilySearch (online collections)

### Key Quirks

1. Two separate colonies until 1691 with distinct record systems
2. Vital registration at town level from 1639 — search by town
3. Plymouth Colony records published and indexed separately
4. Great Migration series (NEHGS) is the essential first stop for 1620–1643 ancestors
5. No census before 1790 — use substitute records
6. County records begin 1643; pre-1643 records at colony level
