## 🗺 Oklahoma Land Run Research Guide (1889–1910)

### Jurisdictional Context

The 1889–1910 period spans **three overlapping jurisdictions** that must be treated separately, because each generated fundamentally different record series:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Apr 22, 1889 | **Land Run opens** the "Unassigned Lands" | No formal territorial government yet |
| May 2, 1890 – Nov 16, 1907 | **Oklahoma Territory** (western/central OK) | Created by Organic Act; capital at Guthrie |
| Pre-Nov 1907 | **Indian Territory** (eastern OK) | Five Civilized Tribes governed this region under separate federal authority |
| Nov 16, 1907 → | **State of Oklahoma** | Two territories merged; statehood begins new record series |

> ⚠️ **The most critical quirk in Oklahoma research:** Before statehood, Oklahoma was split into two entirely separate jurisdictions. Which side your ancestor lived on determines which archives and record series apply. Don't assume a unified "Oklahoma" before 1907.

---

### 1. 🏡 Land Records — The Cornerstone of Land Run Research

**These are the single most important records for 1889 Land Run families.** Every settler who filed a homestead claim generated a multi-document federal file.

**What survives:**
- Homestead application, proof of settlement (including witnesses who knew the family), and final patent
- Rejected and contested applications also survive — these can be rich in family detail
- FamilySearch has a digitized, **indexed** collection: **"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** — 234,567 records with 117,283 images ([FamilySearch Collection 1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872))

**Where held:**
- **National Archives, Washington D.C.** — Record Group 49 (General Land Office records), the authoritative repository for original homestead files
- **BLM General Land Office Records website** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — searchable land patents online, free
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — territorial land-related records

**Access level:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch; name-searchable patents on BLM GLO; original files at NARA require a records request.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Oklahoma Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run); [Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))*

---

### 2. 📊 Census Records

**Federal censuses (1890 mostly destroyed — but Oklahoma is an exception):**
- The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed in a 1921 fire. However, **the 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census is one of the few surviving 1890 enumerations in the nation.** This is a uniquely valuable resource for Land Run families. Held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society** and partially digitized.
- **1900 federal census** — Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory both enumerated; fully indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **1910 federal census** — State of Oklahoma enumerated; fully indexed

**Indian Territory / tribal censuses:**
- FamilySearch has a digitized, indexed collection: **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** — 567,890 records with 283,945 images ([FamilySearch Collection 1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432))

**Access level:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch and Ancestry for 1900/1910; 1890 special census held primarily at OHS.

---

### 3. 📜 Vital Records

**Births and deaths — a major gap in this period:**
- Oklahoma Territory had **no territorial law requiring registration of births or deaths.** No reliable territorial-era birth or death registers exist.
- The FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Oklahoma-specific vital registration start date for the state period; the exact year statewide registration began after 1907 statehood is not confirmed by the tools consulted — check the [Oklahoma Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records) wiki page directly.
- **Substitute sources:** church records (see below), cemetery records, newspaper death notices, and funeral home records are the primary alternatives for 1889–1910 births and deaths.

**Marriages:**
- Marriage records begin with the **earliest Oklahoma Territory counties in 1890** — filed at county courthouses
- FamilySearch has a digitized, indexed collection: **"Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995"** — 456,789 records (913,578 persons) with 228,394 images ([FamilySearch Collection 2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)) ✅ start here
- Indian Territory marriages before 1907 were governed by **tribal courts** — search tribal records, not county courthouses

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Oklahoma Territory Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territory_Records#Vital))*

---

### 4. ⛪ Church Records

Denominations established congregations in the newly opened towns immediately after April 1889. Records are **sparse but do begin in 1889** for some congregations.

- FamilySearch has: **"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** — 123,456 records with 61,728 images ([FamilySearch Collection 1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321))
- For Indian Territory, mission records from Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian missionaries to the Five Tribes can be extensive and predate 1889
- **Denominational archives** (Southern Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, Catholic) hold records not yet digitized
- Oklahoma Historical Society holds some church record collections

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))*

---

### 5. 🪶 Indian Territory & Five Civilized Tribes Records

If any part of your research touches **eastern Oklahoma (Indian Territory)**, this is a distinct and rich record world:

**Dawes Rolls (1898–1914):** The definitive enrollment of Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole citizenship — required for allotment under the Dawes Act. These are among the most genealogically detailed federal records of the era. Indexed and widely available on FamilySearch, Ancestry, and Fold3.

**Other tribal records:**
- **Tribal census rolls** — compiled annually by BIA agents
- **Annuity payment rolls** (1830s–1900s) — list heads of household and sometimes family members; at NARA (Record Group 75, M234), partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3
- **Allotment records and tribal court records**

**Repositories:**
- **National Archives at Fort Worth** — Record Group 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs), the primary repository for Indian Territory federal records
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — extensive tribal records collections
- **Tribal archives** — Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, etc. maintain their own historical records offices

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Five Civilized Tribes Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records))*

---

### 6. ⚖️ Territorial Court Records

For Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907), district courts handled civil, criminal, probate, guardianship, and **naturalization** filings.

- **Pre-1906 naturalizations** could be filed in any court of record — territorial district courts are a key source for immigrant Land Run settlers
- Territorial court records are held at the **National Archives at Fort Worth** and the **Oklahoma State Archives**
- These records include names, origins, and sometimes family details not found elsewhere

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Oklahoma Territory Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territory_Records))*

---

### 7. 💰 Tax Records & School Censuses

- **County tax rolls from the 1890s** document early settlers and property — useful substitute when vital records are absent
- **School censuses** were compiled at the territorial level and name children and parents
- Both are held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society** and **Oklahoma State Archives**

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Oklahoma Territory Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territory_Records))*

---

### 8. 🪖 Military Records

- Service records, pension files, and draft registrations for veterans in this period are at **NARA**
- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) — subscription site with good military record coverage
- Oklahoma had militia and National Guard units; state adjutant general records are at the **Oklahoma State Archives**

---

### 9. 📰 Newspapers

Territorial towns launched newspapers almost immediately after the 1889 Land Run — local papers are a prime source for early settler names, deaths, marriages, and legal notices.

- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) — subscription, broad Oklahoma coverage
- **Chronicling America** ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)) — Library of Congress, free, includes some Oklahoma territorial papers
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** newspaper holdings

---

### 10. 🗂 Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth** | Indian Territory BIA records (RG 75), territorial court records, Dawes Commission files | In-person + some online via Fold3/FamilySearch |
| **NARA, Washington D.C.** | Homestead/GLO files (RG 49), military records | Records requests; GLO patents at glorecords.blm.gov |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | 1890 special census, tax rolls, newspapers, church records, territorial records | [okhistory.org](https://www.okhistory.org); in-person and some online |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** | State government records post-1907, territorial court copies | Part of OK Dept. of Libraries; [odl.state.ok.us](https://www.odl.state.ok.us) |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 indexed collections (land records, Indian censuses/rolls, county marriages, church records) | Free at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses (1900, 1910), Dawes Rolls | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Military records, Dawes Rolls, BIA annuity rolls | Subscription |
| **BLM GLO Records** | Land patents from homestead filings | Free at glorecords.blm.gov |
| **Find A Grave / BillionGraves** | Cemetery records | Free |
| **County Courthouses** | Marriage records (1890+), deed books, probate | In-person or county websites |

---

### ⚠️ Key Research Quirks

1. **Oklahoma Territory ≠ Indian Territory.** Before Nov. 1907, they were separate jurisdictions with different archives. Confirm which one your ancestor lived in before searching.
2. **No territorial vital registration.** Births and deaths in 1889–1907 are almost never in official registers. Use church records, newspapers, and cemetery records instead.
3. **The 1890 special census survived.** Unlike the nationally destroyed 1890 federal census, Oklahoma Territory's special enumeration is one of the few surviving 1890 census records in the country — seek it at the Oklahoma Historical Society.
4. **Trace Land Run settlers back to their origins.** The FamilySearch Wiki notes that many settlers came from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri — search those states' records for the family's pre-Oklahoma life.
5. **Homestead files are multi-document.** Don't stop at the patent — the proof-of-settlement file with witness statements, and even rejected claims, may contain detailed family information.
6. **Indian Territory marriages were tribal, not county.** County marriage records don't apply to Indian Territory before 1907; look to tribal courts and records.
7. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are in territorial district courts.** Immigrant settlers who naturalized before the 1906 Basic Naturalization Act may appear in Oklahoma or Indian Territory district court records at NARA Fort Worth.
8. **Volume_search returned only 1 digitized volume** for this period (tribal enrollment cards for Indian Territory, 940 images, 99% indexed, full-text searchable). Additional Oklahoma volumes may exist but were not surfaced in this survey — browse FamilySearch's [image holdings](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image) directly as a follow-up.

---

**Where to start:** If your ancestor participated in the 1889 Land Run, begin with the **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) for a land patent, then order the full homestead case file from NARA. Pair that with the **1890 Oklahoma Territory special census** and the **FamilySearch land records collection** (1541872) to establish the family in place. Then move to county marriage records and the 1900 census to build forward.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region (1860–1900)
### Schuylkill · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Carbon · Northumberland · Columbia Counties — Irish Immigrant Miners

---

## Jurisdiction Overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **Counties surveyed** | Schuylkill, Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, Columbia |
| **Parent state** | Pennsylvania (admitted 1787) |
| **Administrative center** | Pottsville (Schuylkill); Wilkes-Barre (Luzerne); Scranton (Lackawanna); Jim Thorpe/Mauch Chunk (Carbon); Sunbury (Northumberland); Bloomsburg (Columbia) |
| **Schuylkill County formed** | 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties *(tool-confirmed)* |
| **Key boundary change in period** | Lackawanna County carved from Luzerne County during the target period; verify the exact date — records for the Scranton/Carbondale area before that formation are held under **Luzerne County**, not Lackawanna |
| **Economy** | Hard-coal (anthracite) extraction; collieries, breaker operations, mule haulage; company towns owned by railroad-affiliated coal companies (Philadelphia & Reading, Delaware, Lackawanna & Western, etc.) |
| **Ethnic composition** | Large Irish immigrant community (Famine-era arrivals and their children); also Welsh, English, German, and later Polish/Slovak/Lithuanian arrivals post-1880 |
| **Dominant religious affiliation** | Roman Catholic (Irish and later Eastern European); Methodist/Welsh Baptist (Welsh miners); Presbyterian; Episcopal |
| **Key historical event** | Molly Maguires trials (1875–1877, centered on Schuylkill County); Civil War draft (1863); Lattimer Massacre (1897) |

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Schuylkill County** (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) was stable within the target period; boundaries are unchanged 1860–1900. *(Source: place_search_all, FamilySearch place record)*
- **Lackawanna County** was separated from Luzerne County within the target period. Any event in the Scranton, Carbondale, or Dunmore area that occurred **before** that formation is recorded under Luzerne County — search Luzerne first for all Lackawanna-area families. *(The coal-region wiki page, [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records), lists both Luzerne and Lackawanna as distinct anthracite counties, confirming the split is genealogically significant; verify the exact formation year before searching.)*
- **Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia** county boundaries were stable across the 1860–1900 window; no boundary-change tool results were returned for these counties.

---

## ⭐ Specialized Coal-Region Indexes

*(Sourced directly from the FamilySearch Wiki page **[Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)** — the only wiki page in this survey that returned substantive coal-region–specific content.)*

### Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898
The most important coal-specific finding aid surfaced in this survey. Covers approximately **41,000 colliery workers** across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Each entry includes:
- Occupation (loader, breaker boy, mule driver, etc.)
- Wage rate
- **Parish of origin, where stated** — this is the critical lead for tracing an Irish miner back to Ireland

> **Research note:** The FamilySearch Coal Region Records wiki distinguishes *payroll-derived indexes* (which name individual workers) from *mine-inspection and accident reports* (which are organized by colliery, not person). The Anthracite Index is the payroll-derived type — the more direct genealogical finding aid, especially for immigrant miners whose names were recorded inconsistently in census records.

### Pennsylvania Triennial State Tax Assessments, 1853 onward
Pennsylvania state assessors enumerated coal-region residents **every three years** from 1853. The assessment ledgers list:
- Householder name
- Real estate value
- **Occupation** (e.g., "miner," "laborer," "colliery operator")
- **Nativity, where recorded**

These fill in the years between federal censuses and are especially valuable for 1860s–1880s immigrants who may not appear clearly in census indexes.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Critical gap for this period:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration during 1860–1900. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records, Pennsylvania Genealogy, and Pennsylvania Church Records all returned generic content rather than Pennsylvania-specific registration dates — I cannot quote a precise statewide start date from a tool result. Researchers should not assume civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for this period.
- **Primary substitutes:** Catholic parish baptismal registers, marriage registers, and burial records (see Church Records below) are the *de facto* vital records for Irish miners in this era.
- **County-level marriage bonds/licenses:** Some counties kept marriage license registers pre-statewide registration; the FamilySearch volume survey (see below) found Schuylkill marriage records beginning 1870 in the digitized holdings.

### Church Records — **THE PRIORITY SOURCE**

The [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) wiki confirms that many Catholic parishes in the coal region were **established between 1840 and 1870** to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities.

**Diocesan custody split (critical for access):**
| Period | Diocesan custodian |
|---|---|
| Before 1868 | **Diocese of Harrisburg** (holds pre-1868 baptismal registers) |
| After 1868 | **Diocese of Scranton** (holds post-1868 registers for northeastern PA coal counties) |

> For southern anthracite counties (Schuylkill, Northumberland, Columbia), registers may fall under the Diocese of Allentown (est. 1961, carved from Philadelphia/Harrisburg) or remain with Harrisburg — contact both if in doubt.

**FamilySearch digitized volume (Schuylkill):**
- **007936751** — Church Records, Schuylkill County, 1842–1895; 187 images; **languages: English and German** (some records are in German for German Catholic/Lutheran congregations); **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be read image by image)

**Access:** Contact the Diocese of Scranton Archives (Scranton, PA) for post-1868 registers; Diocese of Harrisburg Archives for pre-1868. Some parishes retain their own registers — write directly to the parish where the ancestor is known to have worshipped.

### Census Records

| Census year | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1860 | Indexed + images | Available on FamilySearch and Ancestry; Schuylkill pop. 89,510 |
| 1870 | Indexed + images | Schuylkill pop. 116,428; first post-Civil War snapshot of the mining community |
| 1880 | Indexed + images | Schuylkill pop. 129,974; **first census to record relationship to household head** — proves family structure; also contains mortality and agricultural schedules |
| 1890 | **Mostly destroyed** | Population schedules largely lost to a 1921 Commerce Dept. fire; only a fragment survives. Use 1889–1892 city directories and triennial tax assessments to bridge the gap |
| 1900 | Indexed + images | Schuylkill pop. 172,927; includes **year of immigration and years in the US** for foreign-born — critical for Irish miners |

*(Source for census content: [Pennsylvania, United States Genealogy — Census Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records))*

**Mortality schedules (1850–1885):** Record persons who died in the year preceding each census — a substitute death record for the pre-registration period.

### Naturalization Records — **HIGH PRIORITY for Irish miners**

Pre-1906 naturalizations are the most informative immigration records because they name the **country of origin** and sometimes the specific townland or county in Ireland.

- **Before September 1906:** Naturalizations were filed in *any court of record* — Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, or Orphans' Court at the county level. Each coal county courthouse holds its own naturalization dockets and indexes separately. An Irish miner could have filed in whichever county he was living in at the time, not necessarily where he lived later.
- **After September 1906:** Centralized in federal courts — **NARA Philadelphia** (Mid-Atlantic Region) holds eastern Pennsylvania federal court naturalizations.
- **FamilySearch volume (Schuylkill):** **007936750** — Naturalization Records, Schuylkill County, 1849–1915; 298 images; **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)

*(Source: [Pennsylvania Naturalization Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records))*

> **Tip:** A miner might have filed a Declaration of Intention ("first papers") in one county and his Petition for Naturalization ("second papers") years later in another. Search all coal counties, not just the one where your ancestor is primarily documented.

### Probate Records

- **FamilySearch collection:** [Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196) — 2,304,118 records / 2,304,118 images. This is a large statewide digitized set covering all counties.
- **FamilySearch volume (Schuylkill):** **007936749** — Probate Records, 1851–1930; 412 images; **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)
- **Held at:** County Register of Wills office (each county courthouse)
- **Value for miners:** Miners who rented company housing and owned little real property may not have probated estates — but *intestate administration files* and *guardianship petitions for minor children* appear even for modest estates and can document family structure when no will was filed.

### Land Records

- **FamilySearch volume (Schuylkill):** **007936752** — Deed Records, 1815–1900; 543 images; **22% name-indexed** (partially searchable by name, images available for the remainder)
- **Pennsylvania is a state-land state** — land grants came from the Commonwealth, not the federal government. County recorder of deeds holds deed books.
- **Company-town context:** Many Irish miners in this period lived in colliery-owned housing and never held a deed. Deed records are more useful for miners who eventually purchased a home lot in the 1880s–1900s. Search deed records for the later part of the period.
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (not rectangular survey)

### Marriage Records

- **FamilySearch volume (Schuylkill):** **007936753** — Marriage Records, 1870–1910; 94 images; **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable)
- County courthouse (Register of Wills or Clerk of Courts depending on county and period)
- For pre-1870 Schuylkill marriages and all marriages in Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia counties: no digitized county marriage volumes appeared in the volume search — treat as **physical only or microfilm only** and contact the respective county courthouse

### Military Records

- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Many Irish miners served in Pennsylvania infantry and artillery regiments. Service records and pension files at **NARA Washington, D.C.** (digitized on Fold3/Ancestry). Pennsylvania contributed over 360,000 men; state-level records at **Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)**.
- **Civil War Draft Records (1863):** Consolidated Lists (Third Series) name all men subject to the draft with age, occupation, and nativity — particularly valuable for Irish miners who may not appear cleanly in other records. Available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Veterans' Schedules (1890):** Although the 1890 population census was mostly destroyed, the **1890 Union Veterans and Widows Schedule** survives separately and is indexed — covers surviving Civil War veterans and their widows.

### Cemetery Records

- Coal-region cemeteries are heavily represented on **FindAGrave** (https://www.findagrave.com). Many Catholic cemeteries operated by the Diocese of Scranton and Diocese of Harrisburg have separate sexton registers.
- **Holy Saviour Cemetery (Pottsville)**, **St. Patrick's Cemetery (Pottsville)**, and their equivalents in Wilkes-Barre, Scranton, Mahanoy City, and Shenandoah are the major Irish Catholic burial grounds.
- Sexton records (often listing death date, age, and sometimes birthplace in Ireland) are held by the individual parishes and dioceses — physical only.

### Newspaper Records

- **The Miners' Journal (Pottsville, 1825–present):** The preeminent anthracite-region newspaper. Rich obituaries, mine accident notices, legal notices, and Irish community news throughout the 1860–1900 period. Available on microfilm at the **Schuylkill County Historical Society** and partially digitized at **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/).
- **The Scranton Tribune / Scranton Republican:** Cover the Luzerne/Lackawanna region; similar obituary and accident coverage.
- **Value for miners:** Mine accident reports often name victims with age and sometimes nativity; obituaries for Irish miners commonly name the townland or parish in Ireland.

### Immigration / Emigration Records

- **Relevant ports of entry:** Most famine-era Irish to the coal region arrived via **Philadelphia** (primary) or **New York/Castle Garden/Ellis Island** (post-1892). Philadelphia passenger lists 1820–1957 are indexed and on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Passenger lists:** Record all persons aboard including infants; examine the full manifest for accompanying family members, neighbors, or townspeople who may share origins.
- **Castle Garden (1855–1892)** and **Ellis Island (1892–1957):** Searchable at www.libertyellisfoundation.org and Ancestry.
- **For 1860s arrivals:** Many Irish miners arrived 1845–1860 during and after the Great Famine; by 1860 they were already in the coal region and their arrival records are at Philadelphia or New York pre-1860.

### Occupational & Company Records — **Coal-Region Specific**

- **Mine inspection reports:** Pennsylvania appointed state mine inspectors beginning in 1869. Annual reports organized by colliery name accidents and fatalities — name, age, cause of death. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**; some digitized. These are organized by colliery, not person.
- **Colliery payroll books:** Where surviving, these are the source for the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index. The original payroll books for many collieries did not survive.
- **Reading Coal & Iron / Philadelphia & Reading Railroad records:** For Schuylkill County collieries, Hagley Museum and Library (Wilmington, DE) holds the Philadelphia & Reading Railroad and Coal & Iron Company records — employment, accident, and property records.
- **Delaware, Lackawanna & Western Railroad records:** For Lackawanna County collieries; contact the **Lackawanna County Historical Society (Scranton)**.
- **Ancient Order of Hibernians (AOH):** The AOH was the primary Irish fraternal organization in the coal region. Membership records can confirm Irish Catholic identity and sometimes county of origin in Ireland. Contact the AOH national archives.
- **Workingmen's Benevolent Association (WBA) / United Mine Workers (UMW, est. 1890):** Union records may survive in labor archives.

### Tax Records

Pennsylvania triennial state tax assessments ran from 1853. These are particularly valuable as census substitutes (especially bridging the destroyed 1890 census gap) and sometimes record nativity. Held at county courthouses and the Pennsylvania State Archives.

## Records NOT Online

The following categories **exist** but were not found in any online database during this survey:

- Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia county naturalization records (digital survey was limited to Schuylkill by the place-resolution tool)
- Catholic parish registers held by the Diocese of Scranton and Diocese of Harrisburg
- Pennsylvania mine inspection annual reports (physical at PA State Archives; not fully digitized)
- Colliery payroll books and company employment records (Hagley and individual county historical societies; few digitized)
- AOH and UMW membership records
- Sexton records for Catholic cemeteries (parish/diocesan custody; physical only)
- City directories for Pottsville, Scranton, Wilkes-Barre, Mahanoy City, Shenandoah (bridging census years)

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1890 Federal Census:** Population schedules mostly destroyed in a 1921 Commerce Department fire; no substitute federal census exists for this year. Bridge with: 1889–1891 city directories; Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments; mine inspection reports; Catholic sacramental registers.
- **Pre-statewide vital records:** No statewide civil birth, marriage, or death registration existed in Pennsylvania during 1860–1900. Records exist only where individual counties or churches maintained them.
- **Colliery payroll books:** The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index notes that the index was drawn from records that "survived a 1903 records consolidation" — many payroll books for other collieries did not survive that consolidation or later company dissolutions.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898** before touching census records — the ~41,000 entries include parish of origin for some miners, which can point directly to the ancestral parish in Ireland. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))*

2. **Distinguish the index types.** Payroll-derived indexes name individual workers; mine-inspection reports are organized by colliery. The Anthracite Index is the payroll type — more useful genealogically. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records — Choosing an Index](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records))*

3. **For the Scranton/Carbondale/Dunmore area:** Search Luzerne County records before searching Lackawanna, because Lackawanna was carved from Luzerne during the target period. Any family event before the county formation date is in Luzerne's records. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) — both counties listed as anthracite counties)*

4. **Church records are your vital records.** Pennsylvania had no statewide civil registration during 1860–1900. Catholic baptismal, marriage, and burial registers — split between the Diocese of Scranton (post-1868) and Diocese of Harrisburg (pre-1868) — are the primary source for Irish miners' vital events.

5. **The 1880 federal census is the most powerful single census for family proof** — it is the first to record the relationship of each household member to the head of household. Work it carefully for every Irish miner household. *(Source: [Pennsylvania, United States Genealogy — Census Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania,_United_States_Genealogy#Census_Records))*

6. **The 1900 census records years of immigration and years in the US** for foreign-born persons — use this to bracket an arrival window, then search Philadelphia or New York passenger lists for that window.

7. **Pre-1906 naturalizations** can appear in Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, or Orphans' Court at any coal county courthouse — and a miner may have filed in a different county from where he ultimately settled. Post-September 1906, go to NARA Philadelphia for federal court records. *(Source: [Pennsylvania Naturalization Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Naturalization_Records))*

8. **Mine accident reports in the *Miners' Journal*** frequently name victims with age and nativity — a death notice substitute when no church burial record or county death record survives.

9. **Use the triennial tax assessments** (Pennsylvania State Archives, from 1853) to bridge the 1890 census gap and to find miners in years when no census was taken.

10. **Five Schuylkill volumes on FamilySearch are browse-only** (naturalization, probate, church, and marriage records). Plan for image-by-image browsing — use the *Miners' Journal* and triennial tax assessments to narrow which years to browse before opening these volumes.

# Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide
### Place: Vermont (future state) · Period: c. 1760–1791

---

## Jurisdictional History

Understanding Vermont's tangled pre-statehood authority is the single most important step in this research, because it determines which jurisdiction created each record and where that record is held today.

| Period | Governing Authority | What to Know |
|---|---|---|
| 1749–1764 | **New Hampshire** (colonial) | NH Governor Benning Wentworth issued 135+ township grants ("New Hampshire Grants") west of the Connecticut River |
| 1764 | **Privy Council ruling** | The Crown ruled the Connecticut River as NY's eastern border — all NH grants were now deemed to lie within New York |
| 1764–1777 | **New York** (claimed) | NY refused to recognize NH grants, re-issued patents, and attempted to enforce authority; settlers (Green Mountain Boys) resisted |
| Jan. 1777 | **Republic of Vermont** declared | Vermont adopted its own constitution (the first in North America to ban slavery) and began creating its own governmental records |
| 1777–1791 | **Republic of Vermont** | Self-governing; created county courts, land records, town clerks, probate districts — these records survive as Vermont's earliest civil archive |
| March 4, 1791 | **14th U.S. State** | Vermont joined the Union; existing Republic-era records rolled into state jurisdiction |

**Key quirk:** Records created before 1791 were made under **three overlapping and competing authorities** — New Hampshire, New York, and the Republic of Vermont. A land transaction in 1775, for example, could involve a NH grant deed, a NY counter-patent, *and* a Vermont proprietors' record all for the same parcel. Search all three streams, not just one.

County formation within the Republic of Vermont began in 1779 (Bennington, Windham, Windsor, Orange, and others). Records for events in early-settled towns may pre-date their county's formal organization and will be found at the **town** level rather than the county level.

---

## What FamilySearch Documents About Vermont's Records

The FamilySearch Wiki's Vermont Genealogy page (`https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy`) is the foundation for this guide. It returns three specific findings for the pre-statehood period:

> **"Vermont, the 14th state (admitted 1791), has a distinctive set of pre-statehood land records that researchers should not confuse with later post-statehood records."**

> **"The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule, prepared under New York colonial authority before statehood, enumerates approximately 1,800 grantees of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists grantee, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. This record predates any Vermont civil registration and is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state."**

> **"Statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857. Earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly; consult town clerk offices directly."**

> **"Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access."**

**Coverage gaps on FamilySearch Wiki:** The specific pages for `Vermont_Vital_Records`, `Vermont_Land_and_Property`, `Vermont_Church_Records`, `Vermont_Probate_Records`, and `Vermont_Census` all returned only generic content when fetched — those Vermont-specific articles either do not exist or are not yet in the wiki system. Consult the [FamilySearch Vermont Research Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy) directly and check the full category listing for any pages added since this guide was produced.

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 1. 🔑 Land Records — **Prime source for this period**

Land records are the single most important record class for pre-statehood Vermont. Civil vital registration did not exist; land was the mechanism through which most residents documented their presence, identity, and family relationships.

**Three parallel streams exist — search all three:**

**A. New Hampshire Grants (pre-1764)**
- Governor Benning Wentworth issued 135+ township charters from 1749–1764, each listing original proprietors by name.
- These charter/grant records are held by the **New Hampshire State Archives** (Concord, NH), not in Vermont.
- Transcriptions appear in *New Hampshire State Papers* (volumes 24–26), which are publicly available.

**B. Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule**
- Prepared under New York colonial authority; enumerates ~**1,800 grantees** of NH grants NY refused to recognize.
- Lists: grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status.
- **FamilySearch identifies this as the earliest systematic resident list for the future state** — begin here if you don't know which town an ancestor lived in.
- Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy

**C. Town Proprietors' Records (Republic of Vermont era, 1777–1791)**
- Each town's proprietors' meeting records document original land divisions, lot assignments, and boundary surveys.
- Held at individual **town clerk offices** and at the **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA)** in Montpelier.
- Many have been transcribed in 19th-century town histories (see below).
- Town deed books from the 1780s onward survive at town clerks' offices and are the primary record of land transfer for this period.

**Digitization status:** `volume_search` and `collections_search` are unavailable in this environment — a specific count of digitized FamilySearch volumes cannot be reported. Check the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) under each Vermont county and town name for microfilmed deed books.

---

### 2. Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths) — **No civil registration in this period**

**The FamilySearch Wiki states statewide civil registration began in 1857** (statewide level). For the pre-statehood window (before 1791), there was **no civil vital registration system** — neither at the statewide level nor at the county level within the Republic of Vermont.

What survives:
- **Town clerk records:** The Wiki notes "earlier town clerk records (some back to the 1770s) survive unevenly." Some towns recorded vital events informally; most did not. Access: contact individual **town clerks** directly — no central index exists for this period.
- **Church registers** (see §4 below) are the primary substitute for vital records.
- **Family bibles**, gravestone inscriptions, and pension files (see §6) also document births, marriages, and deaths.

⚠️ Do not expect a systematic vital record for any pre-1791 Vermont event. If you find one, treat it as a bonus, not the standard.

---

### 3. Census Records

**1790 Federal Census:** Vermont is included in the 1790 federal schedules. Although Vermont did not formally join the Union until March 4, 1791 — after the August 1790 enumeration — Congress authorized a supplemental enumeration of Vermont, and the published 1790 census schedules include all Vermont counties. This is the first systematic federal population count covering the future Vermont, and it is available on Ancestry (general link returned by `external_links_search`: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) and at NARA.

**For the years before 1790:** No federal census exists. The **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (see §1) is the closest equivalent for the pre-Revolution period. For 1777–1790, **tax lists** and **town grand lists** (see §7) partially substitute.

---

### 4. Church Records — **Primary substitute for vital records**

In the absence of civil registration, church registers are the most likely source for baptism (birth), marriage, and burial (death) dates.

**Denominations present in pre-statehood Vermont:**
- **Congregationalist** — dominant in southern and Connecticut River valley towns; often the first church organized in a new settlement
- **Baptist** — significant presence across the territory by the 1780s
- **Episcopal (Anglican/Church of England)** — smaller but present, especially near the New York border
- **Methodist** — beginning to appear by the late 1780s
- **Presbyterian** — some presence, especially among New England migrants

**Where records are held:**
- At individual churches (if the congregation survives)
- At denominational archives (e.g., the Congregational Library & Archives in Boston holds many early New England registers)
- At the **Vermont Historical Society** (Barre, VT), which holds transcriptions and some originals
- FamilySearch has microfilmed some Vermont church registers — check the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) by county or town

⚠️ The FamilySearch Wiki pages for `Vermont_Church_Records` returned only generic content in this survey — no Vermont-specific article was found. Consult FamilySearch Wiki directly and check the [Vermont Historical Society](https://vermonthistory.org/) finding aids.

---

### 5. Probate Records

The Republic of Vermont organized **probate districts** beginning in the late 1770s, generally aligned with counties. Probate records from this period — wills, inventories, letters of administration, guardianship bonds — are among the most genealogically rich pre-statehood documents surviving in Vermont.

**Where held:** Vermont probate court records are held at the **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA)** and at county probate courts. The early records (1778 onward) have been microfilmed.

**FamilySearch Wiki note:** The `Vermont_Probate_Records` page returned only generic content in this survey — check the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) under "Vermont — Probate Records" for available microfilm and any digitized volumes.

---

### 6. Military Records — **Revolutionary War**

Vermont men served in the Continental Army, state militia (as the Republic of Vermont's own forces), and as Green Mountain Boys in earlier actions (1770–1775). The Revolutionary War period (1775–1783) is squarely within your target window.

**Key sources:**
| Record Type | Where Held | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Continental Army service records | NARA (Washington DC) | Microfilm; some indexed online at Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/) |
| Pension and Bounty Land Warrant files | NARA, RG 15 | Fold3 (indexed); these files often contain family detail — spouse names, children, marriage dates, ages |
| Vermont militia records | VSARA and Vermont Historical Society | Check finding aids |
| Compiled Military Service Records (CMSRs) | NARA | Fold3 and Ancestry |

**Pension files are especially valuable** for this period. A widow applying for a pension in the 1820s–1840s had to document her marriage, often producing the only surviving record of a pre-statehood Vermont marriage.

NARA: https://www.archives.gov/ (returned by `external_links_search`)

---

### 7. Tax Records / Grand Lists

Vermont towns maintained annual **grand lists** (tax assessment rolls) listing taxable inhabitants, property, and livestock. These survive from the late 1770s onward for many towns and serve as a census substitute, documenting male heads of household year by year.

**Where held:** Individual town clerk offices and VSARA. Check the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) — some have been microfilmed.

---

### 8. Town Histories

The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly highlights this source class: *"Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access."* (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)

Many of these histories include:
- Proprietors' lists from the original NH grants
- Early settler rosters
- Transcribed vital records from church registers and town books
- Family genealogies submitted by descendants

**Access:** Available at the **Vermont Historical Society**, the **Library of Congress**, and digitized at [HathiTrust](https://www.hathitrust.org/) and [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/). Search by town name.

---

### 9. Cemetery Records / Gravestone Inscriptions

Pre-statehood Vermont cemeteries include many 1770s–1790s stones, some of which record birth places (often Massachusetts or Connecticut — note the heavy migration from southern New England) as well as death dates and family relationships.

- **Find A Grave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) — returned by `external_links_search`; search by Vermont county or town
- **Vermont Old Cemetery Association** has surveyed many early burial grounds
- The Vermont Historical Society holds cemetery transcription volumes

---

### 10. Newspapers

Vermont's earliest newspapers date to the 1780s (*Vermont Gazette*, 1781; *Vermont Journal*, 1783). They carried legal notices, estate advertisements, and occasional vital announcements — rare but worth checking for the late pre-statehood period.

- **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) — returned by `external_links_search`; check Vermont holdings for late 1780s titles

---

## Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA)**, Montpelier, VT | Republic of Vermont records, probate, land records, legislative papers | In person; some records microfilmed at FamilySearch |
| **Vermont Historical Society**, Barre, VT | Town histories, church register transcriptions, manuscripts, cemetery surveys | In person and online finding aids at vermonthistory.org |
| **Individual town clerk offices** | Deed books, grand lists, town clerk vital records (back to 1770s, uneven) | Contact each town directly; no statewide index for pre-1857 records |
| **New Hampshire State Archives**, Concord, NH | Original NH grant charters (Benning Wentworth grants) | In person; *NH State Papers* vols. 24–26 available in print/digitized |
| **New York State Archives**, Albany, NY | NY patents and competing land claims for the disputed territory | In person |
| **NARA** (Washington, DC / various) | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, 1790 census | In person; Ancestry, Fold3, Archival Research Catalog online |

---

## Key Research Quirks for This Period

1. **No civil vital records exist before 1791** (statewide registration began in 1857). Church registers, town clerk informal records, and pension files are the primary substitutes.
2. **Land records under three jurisdictions** — NH grants, NY patents, and Vermont proprietors' records may all cover the same family and parcel. Search all three.
3. **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (~1,800 names) is the earliest systematic resident list for the future state; treat it as your starting census substitute for the 1760s–1770s.
4. **Records are held at the town level, not county level**, for most pre-statehood events. Always identify the specific town — a county-level search alone will miss series recorded by town clerks.
5. **Many Vermont settlers migrated from Connecticut and Massachusetts** in the 1760s–1780s. If you cannot locate a vital record in Vermont, search the origin colony/state — the birth and early marriage record is likely there, not in Vermont.
6. **Vermont was NOT included in the first federal census taken in August 1790** as a formal state, but a supplemental enumeration was conducted and Vermont IS in the published 1790 federal census schedules.
7. **Town histories (1860–1900) frequently reprint proprietors' records** otherwise inaccessible — check these before concluding a record doesn't survive (per FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy).
8. **FamilySearch coverage gap:** `collections_search` and `volume_search` were unavailable during this survey; specific digitized collection counts cannot be reported. Check the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) directly for Vermont county and town entries.

---

## Recommended Starting Sequence

1. **Identify the town.** All pre-statehood Vermont research pivots on the specific town — county alone is insufficient.
2. **Check the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** if you need to place an ancestor in the territory before 1777.
3. **Search the 1790 federal census** (supplemental Vermont enumeration) to establish household composition at the statehood threshold.
4. **Pull the town's deed/land records** at VSARA and the town clerk's office for the 1780s.
5. **Check probate records** at VSARA — wills and inventories from the Republic era survive from 1778 onward.
6. **Identify the church affiliation** (typically Congregationalist in early settled towns) and locate that church's register at the Vermont Historical Society or FamilySearch Catalog.
7. **Search pension files** at NARA/Fold3 if the ancestor or a male relative served in the Revolution — pension widow applications are the richest surviving source for pre-1791 Vermont marriages.
8. **Consult the town history** for your specific Vermont town — the Vermont Historical Society and HathiTrust are the best starting points.

---
